column5: Two documented keys are wrong or missing on the FileChanged stdin payload. (1) Key name only: the absolute-path field is spelled `path`, the doc spells it `file_path` — the value is the same idea, so this is a rename, except that our value is not guaranteed absolute (no `resolve()` against the session cwd) and is absent when uncorrelated. (2) Missing field: `event` (`change`|`add`|`unlink`) is never emitted at all, and the extra `change_kind` (the mutating tool name) is a Nessy invention with no documented counterpart. Because `hookCommandStdinPayload` spreads the input verbatim, a hook doing `jq -r .file_path` reads `null` and `jq -r .event` reads `null`. Separately, and narrower than the doc rather than contradicting a field: the trigger is tool completion over four write tools, not a filesystem watch, so `unlink` is structurally unreachable (a deletion, or any edit made by bash/an external editor, never fires the event), the matcher never builds a watch list, and the documented `watchPaths` output field is unimplemented anywhere in src (`grep -ran watchPaths packages/*/src apps/electron/src` returns nothing).

column8: Observable, and it makes an imported Claude plugin look broken rather than absent. Install a Claude plugin whose `hooks.json` declares a FileChanged hook — the documented example shape is a `.envrc`/`.env` reloader, and formatter-on-save hooks are the same pattern — then have the agent write that file with the write/edit tool. The hook DOES fire and its matcher DOES match (the basename comes from the `path` fallback), so the user sees the hook run and any stderr surface; but the script's `jq -r .file_path` (or `$file_path`) yields the string `null`, so it formats nothing, reloads nothing, or errors on a path named "null". Any `event`-conditional branch (`if [ "$event" = "add" ]`) never takes, since the key is absent on every emission. A user writing their own Nessy automation from our docs hits the same wall from the other side: docs-site documents the event but no fields, so copying a Claude example is the natural move. Latent parts, for honesty: deleting a file, editing one through bash, or an external editor touching a watched file produces no event at all — that surfaces only for a user who expects a real disk watcher, and no `watchPaths`-returning hook can work at all today.

column8: Silent wrong output for one concrete population: a user installs a Claude plugin whose CwdChanged hook reads the documented field — the direnv-style recipe the page itself motivates, e.g. `new=$(cat | jq -r '.new_cwd')`. Today the hook registers, fires on every `cd`, and exits 0, so Sources shows it healthy and the automations run log shows a successful run with no stderr. But `jq` yields `null`, so the environment reload the plugin exists to perform either does nothing or acts on the literal string "null", and the user's per-directory toolchain silently never activates. Same for `.old_cwd` in any hook that diffs the two directories. Nothing tells them why. A native Nessy automation authored against our own field names is unaffected, and users with no Claude CwdChanged plugin see nothing at all — so the blast is narrow, but where it lands it is invisible rather than loud, which is the worse failure mode.

column5: Three deltas, and none of them is a key rename.  1. Firing rule inverted. The doc says Setup does not fire on normal startup and fires only under `--init-only` / `-p --init` / `-p --maintenance`. Nessy fires it on every Pi `session_start` (`lifecycle-bridge.ts:104-107`), i.e. on ordinary startup, which is the exact case the doc excludes. 2. The documented key is absent, not misspelled. The payload carries `source: 'pi-runtime'` and `lifecycle_version: 1` and no `trigger` at all (`lifecycle-bridge.ts:107`, frozen at `automations/types.ts:38`). `source` is not a renamed `trigger`: `pi-runtime` is not one of the two legal values, and `source` is separately the documented matcher field of `SessionStart` (`utils.ts:190-191`), so re-reading `source` as Setup's trigger would collide. 3. The gate the value would come from does not exist. There is no launch mode in the product to derive `init` vs `maintenance` from (`apps/cli/src/index.ts:77-140`), so this cannot be fixed at the emitter alone — the trigger has to be introduced at the CLI and carried to the host.  Downstream of those: Setup's matcher is inert (`utils.ts:238`, `hooks-automation.ts:347`), so an imported Claude Setup hook is all-or-nothing — catch-all hooks over-fire once per session, correctly-matched (`init`/`maintenance`) hooks never fire.

column8: Observable today, in three distinct ways.  1. Over-firing. Install a Claude plugin whose `hooks/hooks.json` has a `Setup` entry with no matcher, and its command runs on EVERY Pi session start — every new chat, and again on any agent dispose+recreate (the `sessionStarted` guard is a fresh closure per `createSession` call, `pi-runtime-adapter.ts:258-272`). hooks.md:1061 reserves this hook for "one-time dependency installation or scheduled cleanup that you trigger explicitly from CI or scripts", so the user pays that work — an `npm install`-class command or a cleanup script — on every chat, as startup latency and repeated disk/network activity, where Claude would have run it once from CI. 2. Silent non-firing of the correct spelling. The same plugin written the documented way, `"matcher": "init"`, never runs at all. The user does get told: the plugin's diagnostics show a warning `plugin.hooks.matcher_never_matches` — "Hook ... declares a matcher on \"Setup\", which has no matcher value in Nessy, so the hook never runs ... Remove the matcher to run on every occurrence" (`hooks-automation.ts:768-777`) — but the only remedy that advice offers is exactly case 1. 3. No maintenance path, and provider-dependent behaviour. There is no `--init-only` / `-p --init` / `-p --maintenance` launch mode anywhere in the product (`apps/cli/src/index.ts:77-140`), so a user cannot run a plugin's cleanup pass at all. And because the Pi bridge is the only emitter, a session on the Claude, Codex or Nestor Cloud backend never fires `Setup` — the same installed plugin behaves differently depending on which model card the user picked.

column8: Concrete and reachable today, on the default Pi runtime.  A user who writes a ConfigChange hook — natively in `hooks.json`, or by installing a Claude plugin that ships one — gets one of two wrong outcomes:  (1) With any documented matcher (`"matcher": "project_settings"`, `user_settings`, `skills`, `policy_settings`, `local_settings`), the hook NEVER runs. Nessy does warn at install/registration time (`plugin.hooks.matcher_never_matches`), so it is not silent, but the hook is dead.  (2) With a catch-all matcher, the hook DOES run — on the wrong occurrences. It fires when the user picks a different model in the composer, changes thinking level, or a connection runtime refreshes; it does NOT fire when they edit `~/.nessy-agent/config.json`, the workspace `hooks.json`/`automations.json`/`permissions.json`, a `SKILL.md`, or when managed gateway settings refresh. The `audit-config-change.sh` recipe printed in hooks.md § ConfigChange therefore writes an audit log with no `source`, no `file_path`, and no settings-file entries at all — it logs model switches instead.  For this fork specifically, the missing occurrence is the one `server-managed-settings.md:277` names as the mechanism to log or block unauthorised changes to managed policy: that tamper-detection path has nothing to fire on. And because the block is advisory (`pi-agent.ts:7331-7341`), even a hook that does fire cannot prevent anything.

column8: Two concrete failures, both on imported plugins that ship hooks (the only surface that can register this event today).  1. The doc's own use case is dead. A user installs a Claude plugin whose `hooks.json` has a `UserPromptExpansion` entry with `"matcher": "deploy"` (block `/deploy` unless an approval file exists). Sources → plugin install shows a warning — "declares a matcher on UserPromptExpansion, which has no matcher value in Nessy, so the hook never runs" (`hooks-automation.ts:767`) — and typing `/deploy` in the composer runs the command with no gate. The guard the user installed silently does nothing.  2. A matcher-less hook fires on the wrong events with an empty payload. It runs once per turn on EVERY prompt, including plain typed messages with no slash command (`pi-agent.ts:6565` → `:6418`), and its stdin JSON contains `{hook_event_name, source: 'pi-before-agent-start', lifecycle_version: 1}` and nothing else. A logging hook records one row per turn instead of one per command and cannot say which command; a gating hook that reads `command_name` sees `undefined` and either no-ops or, if it blocks by default, kills every turn in the session with "A UserPromptExpansion hook blocked this prompt."  Latent third: even with a hook that does block, `/mycommand` has already been expanded server-side by then — for an MCP prompt command the remote `getPrompt` call already happened, and a command carrying `model:` has already switched the session model (sessions.ts:342). The user sees the turn refused but the model in the composer changed anyway.

column5: Three deltas, in descending size. (a) THE NUMBER: our MCP persist threshold is 12,000 estimated tokens, the doc's is 25,000 — so every MCP result in the ~12k–25k token band (roughly 48KB–100KB of plain text) is taken off the model and replaced with a file reference where Claude Code hands it over inline. On the Claude backend and on the local-tools path the effective number is lower still, `min(12000, 10% of the model's context window)` with a 2,000-token floor, because the second guard passes `contextWindow`. (b) THE OVERRIDE IS ABSENT, not misnamed: there is no `MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS` and no `NESSY_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS` — nothing reads any env var here, so a user who follows Claude's docs and exports `MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS=50000` gets no effect whatsoever. column8: Concrete and reachable today. Call any MCP tool that returns a mid-sized text payload — a GitHub issue list, a DB schema dump, a Confluence/Jira page fetch, a `tools/list`-style inventory — sized roughly 48KB–100KB. In Claude Code the agent receives it inline; in Nessy the chat shows the tool returning a `[Response too large]`-style replacement naming a `long_responses/…txt` path plus an LLM summary, and the agent has to spend an extra turn Reading the file back, with whatever the summary dropped simply gone from the turn. On the Claude backend, or any model with a context window under 120k, it bites earlier still — the second guard scales the limit to 10% of the window (floor 2,000 tokens), so an ~8KB MCP result already spills on a 64k-window model. And the documented escape hatch does not exist: a user who reads Claude's docs and exports `MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS=50000` sees exactly no change, with no warning that the variable is unrecognised. Separately, a server that declared `anthropic/maxResultSizeChars` to keep its big result inline gets that honoured by the pool and then undone one layer up on the Claude and local-tools backends, so the annotation appears not to work.

column5: Two wrong strings on the ingress, plus one field that has nowhere to go. (1) The registered method literal is `claude/channel` where the contract says `notifications/claude/channel` — the value we used is real, but it is the capability key, not the method, so the prefix is simply missing. (2) The param read is `params.text` where the contract says `params.content` — again only the key name is wrong; the value's meaning, sanitization and 32 KiB bound are all correct and can be kept as-is. (3) `meta` is absent at the type level, not merely unread: `McpChannelMessage` carries no field for it and the pool guard would reject nothing but also preserve nothing. Because MCP dispatch is an exact string map with no fallback handler here, (1) alone means a doc-conforming channel server has every event dropped with no error and no log; (2) means even a server that used our un-prefixed method would still be ignored unless it happened to send `text`. Nothing in the repo emits either form (`grep -arn 'claude/channel'` over source finds only client.ts:113 plus prose in docs-site), so there is no in-house producer to stay compatible with.

column8: Observable, and it is exactly the everyday case of a team skill checked into a repo. A user who keeps `deploy` in `~/.nessy-agent/skills/` (or `~/.agents/skills/`) and opens a project that ships `.nessy-agent/skills/deploy` (or `.agents/skills/deploy`) loses the bare name to the project's copy: the skill listing handed to the model advertises the PROJECT skill as `deploy` and the personal one only under a long qualified key (packages/shared/src/agent/core/prompt-builder.ts:122), and a bare `[skill:deploy]` — typed in prose or emitted by the model — runs the project's version (packages/shared/src/agent/base-agent.ts:2124-2126). On Claude the personal skill wins. Nothing warns the user: the collision is recorded at info severity only (packages/shared/src/capabilities/resolver.ts:2056-2061) and no surface renders it. Worse, the same word means two different skills in two surfaces today — `/deploy` in the slash menu resolves to the personal skill (first-listed entry claims the name, packages/shared/src/slash-commands/custom-commands.ts:441-448) while the bare mention resolves to the project one, so a user who checks the menu and then types the name gets a different skill than they picked. Latent only until a name collides across levels; no impact for users with no personal skills.

column8: Concrete and reachable: install or author a skill whose name matches an existing command file — `review`, `deploy`, `fix-issue`, exactly the generic names Claude's own docs use as examples — and the skill vanishes from the `/` menu. The user sees one `/review`, picks it, and gets the `commands/review.md` prompt instead of the skill; there is no second, namespaced `/review` row to reach the skill from, because the skill is dropped before it is pushed (custom-commands.ts:444 vs :447). The only remaining routes are model auto-invocation or hand-typing the `[skill:review]` marker, neither of which is discoverable from the composer. Same effect from a workflow recipe of that name. A user following Claude's documentation ('shadow the command with a skill of the same name') gets the opposite of what the page promises, silently — no diagnostic is logged for the drop.

column5: Two deltas, both on the same knob. (1) VALUE: our default ceiling is 1 where the page says 3 — i.e. we ship Claude's documented "turn nesting off" setting as the unconditional product behaviour. (2) NO OVERRIDE PATH: `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH` has no `NESSY_`-prefixed counterpart, and the `orchestrator.depth` knob that would carry it (`pi-agent-server/README.md:47`) is never populated by host code, so the ceiling is fixed at 1 rather than merely defaulted to 1. The key names and the wire shape are right — `PiOrchestratorConfig.depth` and `budgets.maxDepth` already exist, are validated and are honoured end to end; only the default value and the reader that feeds it are missing. Not a naming mismatch, not a missing mechanism: an enforcement path that works, set to the wrong number with nothing able to change it. The value was deliberately chosen for parity when the page documented a default of 1 (v2.1.217-218); the page moved to 3 in v2.1.219 and we did not.

column7: Crosses a WIRE boundary and a PERSISTENCE boundary — a risk trigger in this repo. `depth` rides the signed Pi execution manifest (`PiOrchestratorConfig`, harness-manifest.ts:31) from server-core to the pi-agent-server subprocess, and the derived `budgets.maxDepth` rides `PiChildStartInput` (`packages/shared/src/agent/pi-harness/child-session-port.ts:7-8`) and is persisted in the child-session record and session JSONL (see `packages/shared/src/sessions/__tests__/jsonl-permission-mode-normalization.test.ts:177`). Host-side revalidation is `packages/server-core/src/pi-harness/child-session-service.ts:574-576`, which rejects `depth > maxDepth` as 'child-session-budgets-invalid' — consistent after the change because the subprocess mints both from the same config. Readers of the value: spawner.ts:518 (refusal) and :602 (child budgets); SessionManager.ts:11141 (inherited.maxDepth on nested starts) and :4932 (plugin-hook path). Manifest-identity checks that must not be tripped: `packages/shared/src/agent/pi-agent.ts:1685-1689` pins the orchestrator the live subprocess was initialized with and fails `register_tools` with 'orchestrator mismatch' if a mid-session refresh shifts it — so the new value must come from a source that is stable for the session's lifetime (an env read at seed time is; a user-toggled setting would need the same generation discipline). `packages/shared/src/agent/__tests__/pi-agent-init-contract.test.ts:207` asserts the literal source text `'maxDepth: config.orchestrator?.depth'` and will break if that line is reshaped. NOT affected: the pinned model-contract hashes — `piStaticModelContractPinKey` (harness-manifest.ts:312) branches only on `forkSubagent`, so raising depth cannot produce 'Pi execution manifest model contract mismatch'. Companion behaviour that changes what a user actually sees: the child tool pool. `packages/pi-agent-server/src/orchestrator/runtime-agent-definitions.ts:33-39` strips ORCHESTRATION_TOOLS (including `subagent`) from a tool-LESS imported descriptor's inherited ceiling (:140-:141), so raising the ceiling alone does not let a default imported agent nest; an agent that names `Agent`/`Task` explicitly resolves through `PI_RUNTIME_AGENT_TOOL_ALIASES` (`packages/shared/src/agent/pi-harness/runtime-agent-definition.ts:31`) and does get `subagent`, as does every fork (spawner.ts:332-353 inherits the session pool). Other suites that assert depth-1 budgets and should be swept: `packages/server-core/src/sessions/SessionManager.child-partial-output.test.ts:22`, `SessionManager.auth-retry-lifecycle.test.ts:69`, `packages/pi-agent-server/src/harness/orchestrator-pin.test.ts:52`.
column8: Concrete and reachable today, on two surfaces. (1) A user installs a Claude plugin whose agent declares `tools` including `Agent` (a reviewer that fans out to verifiers is the doc's own example), the main session delegates to it, and that agent's first `subagent` call comes back `Subagent depth limit exceeded (1)`. The failed tool call shows only inside the subagent's own transcript; the main conversation just gets a thinner summary, so it reads as the agent choosing not to delegate rather than as a refusal. (2) With `NESSY_FORK_SUBAGENT=1`, a fork inherits the session's exact tool pool, so `subagent` is listed for it and returns the same error at the first nested call. Same for any `workflow` script running inside a subagent — every `agent()` call fails (workflow-tool.ts:605 passes the session depth). (3) An admin who copies Claude's documented `settings.json` env entry, in either spelling, gets no effect at all: nothing reads it, and there is no UI, setting or config file that raises the ceiling either — `orchestrator.depth` is documented in the pi-agent-server README as a knob but no host path populates it. What stays invisible: an imported agent that declares no `tools` never receives `subagent` in the first place (ORCHESTRATION_TOOLS strip), so for that shape the depth limit is latent behind an earlier one.

column5: The value is wrong, not the key: `args` is spelled correctly and reaches the script correctly whenever it is supplied — the only delta is the substitution performed when it is NOT supplied. Claude leaves the global `undefined`; we hand the script `{}` (workflow-tool.ts:750 and :660), and on the slash path we hand it `{ input: '' }` (sessions.ts:337-340). Consequence: every documented no-input branch (`args === undefined`, `!args`, `args ?? default`) is unreachable, because `{}` is both defined and truthy. In the opposite direction our behaviour is more lenient than the spec — `args.foo` yields `undefined` here where Claude throws a TypeError — so no script errors out; it silently takes the wrong branch.

Tests that touch this: workflow-tool.test.ts:48-50 (breaks, see change list), workflow-tool.test.ts:111-130 (passes args explicitly, unaffected), sandbox.test.ts:16/72/89/199 (all pass `args` explicitly, unaffected), workflow-real-server.test.ts:326 and :428-429 and packages/shared/src/agent/__tests__/pi-agent-slash-workflow-turn.test.ts:118 (fixtures that construct `args: { input: '' }` themselves — unaffected by the tool fix; only the sessions.ts edit changes what production builds). Imported-plugin path: Claude plugin `workflows/` scripts are imported verbatim (packages/shared/src/plugins/format-adapters/claude.ts:157, :314, :2606) and dispatch through SessionManager.ts:16158 into the same runtime, so the behaviour change applies to third-party Claude-authored scripts too. Behaviour-change risk worth naming: a script already written against today's `{}` that does `args.input` unconditionally will start throwing `Cannot read properties of undefined` instead of silently reading undefined — that is the documented Claude behaviour, but it is a change for scripts saved before the fix.
column8: Today, running a saved or plugin workflow with no input never takes its no-input path. Concretely: the user types `/release-audit` in the composer with no trailing text; the RPC layer sends `args: { input: '' }` (sessions.ts:337-340) and, on the tool-call route, the runtime substitutes `{}` (workflow-tool.ts:750). A script written to Claude's documented idiom — `const target = args ?? 'HEAD'`, or `if (!args) { return usage() }`, or `const files = args === undefined ? await discover() : args.files` — silently takes the has-input branch and runs against `{}`/`''`: agents get prompts with a blank target, a fan-out over an empty list produces zero or one empty item, and the run reports success. No error surfaces anywhere, so the user sees a workflow that 'ran' and did nothing useful, with nothing in the transcript naming the cause. This is not hypothetical for imported content — Claude plugin workflows are loaded verbatim and are exactly the scripts written to that page's idiom. For workflows our own model authors it is latent, because the prompt guidance tells it to read `args.input` (workflow-tool.ts:410, :413) rather than to branch on absence.

column5: Two deltas, both on the same doc sentence, plus one absent knob. (a) VALUE: the nesting budget defaults to 1 where the page says 3. Depth 1 is precisely Claude's documented 'nesting off' setting, so we ship the off configuration as the default. Nothing about the mechanism, the field name (`orchestrator.depth` → `budgets.maxDepth`) or the enforcement point is wrong — only the number. (b) MISSING OVERRIDE: `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH` has no reader and no Nessy-spelled equivalent, so the value cannot be changed by a user at all; the doc's `settings.json` `env` example has no effect. This half is not-built, not mis-valued. (c) WITHHOLDING RULE INVERTED IN SCOPE: the page withholds `Agent` from a subagent AT THE LIMIT; we subtract `subagent` from every tool-less subagent's inherited pool at every depth (`runtime-agent-definitions.ts:141`) and, for an agent that names it explicitly, return `Subagent depth limit exceeded (1)` at call time — which is the page's FORK behaviour applied to named subagents. At today's limit of 1 the two layers happen to agree; raising (a) alone would change nothing observable, because (c) still keeps `Agent` out of every default subagent's pool. That coupling is the reason this is one fix and not two.

column8: Observable, and it looks like a product limitation rather than a setting. A subagent cannot delegate at all today, on two surfaces. (1) The common case is silent: a user's or an imported plugin's agent that declares no `tools` list never receives the `Agent`/`subagent` tool, so a reviewer subagent asked to 'dispatch a verifier per finding' simply does the whole job itself in one context — the user sees a flatter, slower, more context-hungry run and no error explaining it. (2) The explicit case is a visible tool error: an author who lists `Agent` in the agent's `tools` gets `Subagent depth limit exceeded (1)` back from the first delegation, mid-run, in the subagent's transcript. Either way there is no setting to change it — putting `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH` in a settings `env` block (the exact remedy the page prescribes) does nothing, because nothing reads it. Users porting a Claude Code workflow that relies on nested delegation get a different result shape with no diagnostic.

column8: Observable, on the fan-out that Nessy advertises. The effective subagent cap is `min(16, cores - 2)`: 6 on a typical 8-core laptop, 2 on a 4-core one. A `subagent` parallel call with 12 tasks starts 6 and silently queues the other 6 — no error, no badge, no reason shown — so a wave Claude Code would run at once takes two or three, and the model, never seeing a refusal, keeps requesting fan-outs the machine will serialize. There is no user or admin knob to raise it. Worse and sharper: `/subtask` blocks. `startSubtaskFork` awaits admission (subtask.ts:137-142) through the same semaphore, so while a background fan-out holds every slot, the user's `/subtask` produces no fork panel and no error until a slot frees — the doc's exact promise is that this fork is 'never blocked by the limit'. Nothing in the product ever prints `Concurrent subagent limit reached`.

column8: Observable today, and it presents as a hard product limitation rather than a setting. A subagent cannot delegate at all: the ceiling is one layer below the main conversation and there is no way for a user to lift it. Two surfaces. (1) The common case is silent — an agent (the user's own or one imported from a Claude/Codex plugin) that declares no `tools` list never receives `subagent` at all (`runtime-agent-definitions.ts:141`), so a reviewer agent asked to "dispatch a verifier per finding" quietly does the whole job itself in one context: the user sees a flatter, slower, more context-hungry run and no message explaining why. (2) The explicit case is a visible mid-run tool error — an author who lists `subagent`/`Agent` in the agent's `tools` gets `Subagent depth limit exceeded (1)` back from the first delegation, in the subagent's transcript. In both cases the documented remedy does not work: setting `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH` (or any Nessy spelling) in the environment or a settings `env` block has no effect, because nothing reads it — a user porting a Claude Code setup that relies on a two- or three-layer agent tree gets a silently flattened run with no diagnostic and no knob.

column8: Observable, but narrow and only on the Pi backend. Today a user who follows Claude's docs and puts `"deny": ["TaskStop"]` (or `"ask"`) in a `.claude/settings.json` we import gets a rule that installs and matches nothing: the tool is neither removed from the model's context nor gated, so the agent can still abort the user's background subagents and workflows despite the deny, and the mismatch warning goes only to `debug()` — there is no surfaced startup warning to catch it. On the managed/admin tier the failure is louder and the opposite direction: `managed-policy.ts:1034-1037` refuses any rule raising `claude_rule.unknown_tool`, so an administrator's `deny TaskStop` is stripped from the policy at load and reported as dropped. Third, a plugin or settings hook whose `PreToolUse`/`PostToolUse` matcher is `TaskStop` never fires on this tool, because the payload's `tool_name` is `stopTask`. Fourth and cosmetic: the transcript labels the call `stopTask`, a name that appears in no documentation the user can read. What makes it narrow is that nobody would guess `stopTask` on their own, so today the only way to write a working rule is to read our source — the documented spelling is the one that fails.

column5: Not a key-name or value error: the sentinel string, the splice position semantics and the replace-on-absence semantics are all implemented correctly in `resolveAutoModeList`. What is missing is the operand — there are no built-in `environment`/`hard_deny`/`soft_deny`/`allow` lists in this fork to splice, and the sole production call site passes no `defaults`. Consequence in both documented directions: (1) including `"$defaults"` splices nothing, so a managed `['$defaults','x']` and a managed `['x']` produce byte-identical judge input, and the sentinel is silently swallowed with no drop record and no diagnostic; (2) omitting `"$defaults"` discards nothing, because the built-in taxonomy is unconditional prose in the judge's system prompt rather than one of the four addressable lists, so the Danger case at :212 is unreachable. The fork is therefore fail-safe on enforcement (no built-in protection is ever lost) and wrong on configuration (the documented splice is a no-op, and the documented take-full-ownership escape hatch does not exist).

column8: For the documented add-your-own-rules case: none observable. An administrator who ships the page's example (`"soft_deny": ["$defaults", "Never run migrations outside the migrations CLI"]`) in the host-owned managed policy gets exactly the guardian behaviour they would get without the sentinel — verified by probe, the two produce a byte-identical judge task — and no protection is lost, because the built-in taxonomy is in the judge's system prompt regardless. What IS observable is the take-full-ownership case the Danger callout describes: an admin who deliberately omits `"$defaults"` to drop a built-in rule — e.g. a team that force-pushes feature branches routinely and wants the built-in destructive-git soft block gone — still gets it applied, so in `auto` mode those pushes keep being routed to a human prompt with a guardian objection, and the only workaround is to add a counter-entry to `allow`. Latent today because the fork has no delivered managed policies in the wild that use the sentinel; it surfaces the moment one does.

column5: The tool-name → allow mapping is correct for the read-only class and wrong for the state-changing class: the classification step chrome.md:106 requires simply does not exist in the permission path, so all 32 verbs collapse onto one verdict. Three separate deltas. (1) In `plan`, state-changing verbs (open, navigate, click, click-at, drag, fill, type, select, upload, set-clipboard, paste, key, scroll, back, forward, evaluate, window-resize, focus, release, close, hide) must prompt and instead run silently. (2) chrome.md:111's batch rule is unimplemented: a semicolon batch is admitted on the tool name, so `snapshot; click @e1` runs promptless even though one action inside it changes state. (3) The doc's per-input-flag refinement has no analogue to violate in our verb set — our `console`/`network` readers have no `clear` and `screenshot` has no `save_to_disk` (`browser-tool-runtime.ts:1194-1237, 1322-1352, 1376-1418`) — so that clause costs nothing today but must not be re-introduced when a flag like `--clear` is added. Not a wrong key name and not a wrong value: the input is never read at all. Separately (NOT bound by chrome.md, which is plan-mode-only): the same two allows make `default` mode promptless for browser calls too, which contradicts mode-manager's own comment at :2178-2184 calling the browser tool 'PERMISSION-REQUIRED per tools-reference.md' twenty lines before allowing it unconditionally — and that citation is itself stale, because `tools-reference.md` fetched 2026-08-03 (465 lines) carries no browser or Chrome row at all.

column8: Real and reachable by default, not latent. The browser tool ships enabled (`browserToolEnabled` default `true`, `packages/shared/src/config/storage.ts:179`) and is exposed in plan mode. A user presses SHIFT+TAB into Plan mode — whose whole promise is 'look, don't touch' — and asks the agent to investigate a page in the Browser pane. The agent may click buttons, fill and submit forms, upload local files to a file input, write the clipboard, navigate away, resize/close the window, or run arbitrary JavaScript via `evaluate` against a page where the user is already logged in, and the user is never asked: no approval row appears in the conversation, and no 'don't ask again' choice is offered because no prompt is raised. The overlay does light up for those verbs (`packages/server-core/src/domain/browser-tool-detection.ts:34-42`), so the user watches it happen after the fact instead of approving it beforehand. The same holds in `default` mode, where a plain-language expectation of an approval prompt for a state-changing browser action is likewise never met. The exposure is highest with a real logged-in browser session, where a single promptless `evaluate` can read cookies and page content and post them off-host.

column8: Concrete and security-relevant. Pick your home folder as a session's project folder or as a workspace default project (Chat working-directory picker, or Settings → Workspace → Default project folder), click Trust once in the dialog, and the grant is written to disk forever: every later launch silently loads and executes everything project-scope under the whole home tree — `~/.nessy-agent/hooks.json` hook commands, `~/.nessy-agent/mcp.json` servers, project skills/agents/permissions (native-sources.ts:995-1024), project `.nessy-agent/config.toml` defaults, and Pi LSP provisioning — with no re-prompt. In Claude Code that same click lasts one session and the dialog comes back next launch. Because the home tree is where every unrelated repo, download and cache lives, this is the one directory where a persisted grant has effectively unbounded reach. The user sees nothing to tell them apart: the dialog and the trusted badge look identical to a normal project's.

Not covered by the row but worth stating so nobody thinks the flag alone closes it: `run` never prints the session id, so a kept session has no user-visible handle.

column8: Two observable failures today. (1) A headless run's session is destroyed: after `nessy-general-agent run "…"` exits, the session is absent from the Nessy Desktop sidebar, `sessions` cannot list it and `send <id>` cannot continue it, and the removal is a hard durable-storage delete (`SessionManager.ts:14950-14952`), so the transcript is unrecoverable — including on Ctrl+C, which destroys the partial run (`apps/cli/src/index.ts:800`). Anyone porting a Claude Code CI recipe that inspects or resumes a `-p` run afterwards loses the data silently, with exit code 0. (2) Worse and immediately visible: passing the documented flag poisons the prompt. `nessy-general-agent run --no-session-persistence "audit this repo"` does not error on the unknown flag — `:160-165` pushes it into `rest` and `:766`/`:424` join `rest` into the prompt, so the model receives "--no-session-persistence audit this repo" and the session is deleted anyway. The user sees a run that answered a slightly wrong question and left nothing behind. Latent third: even `--no-cleanup` today gives no usable handle, because a text-mode run never prints the session id.

column5: Not a key-name or value mismatch — a missing state transition plus a validator that forbids it.  (a) On `parsed.complete === true` we write verdict `complete_suggested` and keep `status: 'active'` (goal-service.ts:248-259) where the page requires clearing the goal and recording an achieved entry. The correct enum value already exists in every schema (`completed` / `status: 'complete'`), so no wire type changes; only which value the evaluator branch produces. (b) Even if (a) were flipped, `validTerminalState` (:555) would reject the record on reload because it demands `evaluation.source === 'manual'`. So the fix is two edits in one file, not one line. (c) The evidence invariant the page implies is already satisfied on the evaluator path: `parseEvaluatorResult` calls `evidenceList(record.evidence, record.complete)` (:498), so `complete: true` with empty evidence is already downgraded to `not_complete` (locked by goal-service.test.ts:154-155). Nothing new is needed there. (d) The "records an achieved entry in the transcript" half is entirely absent — no transcript/receipt entry and no `['goal']` domain invalidation is emitted when a goal terminates. (e) Wider than filed: the page's whole premise (the USER types a condition, a FRESH model decides completion) has no surface here. There is no `/goal`, no `/goal clear`, no status view; only the model can create a goal, and only the model can complete it — the loop is model-owned end to end. (f) Narrower than filed in one respect, and this is a deliberate superset, not a defect: our extra spend is capped by budgets (goal-service.ts:14-19, :284) where Claude's `/goal` is uncapped. Keep it. (g) Cosmetic only: `MAX_CONDITION` is 8_192 (goal-service.ts:21) against the documented 4,000-character limit (:72) — more permissive, no user-visible divergence.

column8: Pi sessions only, and only after the model has set a goal with the pi-only `Goal` tool — there is no way for a user to set one. When it happens: the evaluator says the condition is met and the session KEEPS WORKING. SessionManager dispatches another full billed turn shown as "Continue active goal (<id>@<rev>)" (SessionManager.ts:3388, :3398), carrying `Last evaluation: complete_suggested: <reason>` in the prompt, and keeps dispatching after every settlement until the model itself calls `Goal complete` or a budget trips. So a goal whose work is demonstrably finished can burn turns up to 32 turns / 250k tokens / $20 / 2h and then end as `budget_exhausted` rather than complete — a successful goal recorded as a budget failure. The user has no way to see or stop this short of stopping the session: no `/goal` command, no status view, no achieved entry in the transcript, and no UI reads `PiHarnessRuntimeSnapshotV1.goal`. What they experience is an agent that will not stop and a chat that keeps producing turns with no visible reason. Whether it surfaces at all depends on the model volunteering `Goal complete` promptly — in the common case it costs one extra turn, in the bad case it costs the whole budget.

column8: Live and severe today, on three surfaces. A `nessy://action/new-session?input=<attacker text>&send=true` link — on any web page, in a Slack/wiki message, in a page opened in Nessy's own browser pane, or rendered as a markdown link inside an assistant message — creates a session on one click and sends the attacker's prompt to the model roughly 100 ms later. The user sees a new chat appear with a message they did not write, already being answered; there is no confirmation, no `Prompt from an external link` warning, and nothing to cancel before the turn starts. The same link can set the new session's permission mode, and `parsePermissionMode` accepts `bypassPermissions` (also spelled `allowall` or `execute`), so the auto-sent prompt can run in the mode that does not ask before tool use. Sibling links are destructive without any prompt at all: `nessy://action/delete-session/<id>` deletes a session, `nessy://action/delete-source/<id>` removes a source, `nessy://action/set-mode/<sessionId>?mode=bypassPermissions` flips an existing session out of its permission mode, and `nessy://action/oauth/<sourceSlug>` starts a sign-in flow. Session ids are guessable enough for a shotgun link, and the markdown-link surface means model output that quotes a fetched web page is itself a delivery path. Nothing in the UI distinguishes any of this from a link the user's own app generated.

column8: Concrete but quiet. Any user whose `MEMORY.md` (global `~/.nessy/MEMORY.md`, the project one, `.nessy-agent/MEMORY.md`, or the per-session file) has grown past 200 lines or 25KB has every byte of it injected into the pinned capability block on every turn of both shipping backends, and re-injected after each compaction (`base-agent.ts:944-957`). What they see is not an error but a budget: higher input token usage per turn, earlier auto-compaction, and — for a file near the 256KB the cleanup guard tolerates (`memory-cleanup.ts:33`) — tens of thousands of tokens per turn of memory they were told would be trimmed at 200 lines. The documented guidance ('keep it under 200 lines, the rest is dropped') is silently false here in the generous direction, so nobody hits a wall; they just pay. It would surface immediately in a token-usage readout comparing a 200-line and a 2000-line MEMORY.md on the same prompt, or in the context-usage indicator after adding a large memory file.

column5: The value, not the mechanism: SIGTERM must exit 143 and exits 130. Both signals share one handler with a constant exit code, so a supervisor cannot distinguish an operator Ctrl-C from an infrastructure shutdown. SIGINT's 130 is already correct and must stay. Registering ANY handler is what breaks it — Node/Bun's default SIGTERM disposition already yields 143; the explicit `process.exit(130)` overwrites the correct number. Positive control on this rig, both runtimes: a script using our exact pattern exits 130 on SIGTERM, the same script with the two `process.on` lines removed exits 143 (node 130/143, bun 130/143). The sentence's other three clauses (abort the turn, terminate the Bash process tree via the server teardown, run SessionEnd) are already satisfied through the cancel + child-SIGTERM path above and are NOT part of this divergence.

column8: Observable today, on the first SIGTERM. Anyone running `nessy-general-agent run <prompt>` under a supervisor — `kill`, `systemd` stop, `docker stop`, a Kubernetes pod eviction, a GitLab CI job cancel or timeout, or an SDK host closing the session — gets exit status 130 instead of 143. Two concrete consequences: a wrapper written to the near-universal SIGTERM convention (`if [ $? -eq 143 ]`, or shell `$((128+15))`) never matches, so an infrastructure-initiated shutdown is reported as a generic failure; and a pipeline that treats 130 as 'the operator cancelled, do not alert' silently swallows a real timeout kill or eviction, because our 130 now means SIGINT, SIGTERM and the streamed `interrupted` event all at once. SIGINT/Ctrl-C behaviour is correct and unaffected.

column5: Two separable deltas, both on the settings-parse boundary; the enforcement half is correct and untouched. (a) KEY NAME AND NESTING. Three of the doc's four path keys are spelled differently and live one level up: `filesystem.allowWrite` -> `additionalWritableRoots`, `filesystem.denyWrite` -> `deniedWriteRoots`, `filesystem.denyRead` -> `deniedReadRoots`. The VALUES, the merge semantics and the enforcement are right — allowWrite/additionalWritableRoots grants and concatenates, the two deny lists restrict and ride the floor, and the resolved lists reach the OS profile correctly. Only the accepted spelling is wrong, which is why the fix is an accepted-alias widening and not a rewrite. `filesystem.allowRead` and `filesystem.allowManagedReadPathsOnly` and `filesystem.disabled` are already correct, so the object is half-conformant, which is what makes the rejection surprising. (b) PATH PREFIXES. The sentence the finding quotes is about prefixes, and none of the three non-absolute prefixes is implemented for ANY of these keys, including the two whose names are already right: `~/` is not expanded, `./` and bare are not resolved against a scope root, and `//abs` is accepted but never normalized to `/abs`. So even a user who translates the key names by hand cannot write `~/.aws/credentials` or `.`, the doc's own examples. Consequence differs by tier and neither is an app failure: at USER scope the strict parse throws and `getUserSandboxSettings` (storage.ts:1293) catches it, logs "[settings] Invalid `sandbox` in the user config — the layer is rejected whole and ignored" (storage.ts:1239) and returns `{}` — the whole `sandbox` layer is inert while the rest of `config.json` applies; at MANAGED scope nothing throws and the tolerant sink strips PER KEY, so `excludedCommands` and `network` still apply while the write/read boundary silently disappears. Adjacent and out of this finding's scope but rejected by the same probe: `sandbox.enabled`, `sandbox.autoAllowBashIfSandboxed`, `sandbox.credentials` (:421-423), `network.allowUnixSockets` and `network.allowLocalBinding` are all unknown keys too.

column8: Concrete and reachable today. An administrator or user copies the sandbox stanza straight out of `settings-reference.md#sandbox`'s worked example (re-anchored 2026-08-29: `settings.md` SPLIT and the sandbox keys moved, so `settings.md:460-478` is dead at the PAGE level; the example still opens `"sandbox": { "enabled": true, "autoAllowBashIfSandboxed": true, …` with a `filesystem.allowWrite` list) into `~/.nessy-agent/config.json`. Nothing about the app fails, and nothing in the UI says anything: the strict parse throws on the FIRST unknown key (`enabled`), `getUserSandboxSettings` swallows it and prints one line to the process console — "[settings] Invalid `sandbox` in the user config — the layer is rejected whole and ignored: invalid sandbox setting: enabled" — and returns an empty layer. Every sandbox setting in that stanza is inert: the extra writable paths, the credential deny, the domain allowlist, all of it, while the rest of `config.json` keeps working normally so the file looks accepted. The same document delivered as MANAGED policy is worse because it degrades PARTIALLY: `excludedCommands` and the whole `network` block apply while `filesystem.allowWrite` and `filesystem.denyRead` are stripped as drops — the admin's write and read boundary vanishes and the policy still looks applied. And a user who correctly translates the key names by hand still cannot write the doc's own path examples: `~/.aws/credentials`, `~/.kube`, `./output` and `.` are each refused with `sandbox-<key>-not-absolute`, so only fully absolute paths under Nessy-only key names work. column5: Two deltas, and neither is a key-name mismatch — the value is wrong AND the model id is never an input.  1. `:454` value/axis. Every effort-capable model defaults to `medium` here; the page requires `high` on all of them and `xhigh` on Opus 4.7. There is no per-model table, no `defaultEffort` on `ModelDefinition`, and no model parameter on `resolveEffortLevel`. `clampThinkingLevelToModel` is model-aware but is the wrong rule: it narrows a chosen level and never supplies one.  2. `:456` hold — not built at all. The persisted level cannot distinguish "the user chose this" from "this was inherited" (`config.defaultThinkingLevel` is one string written by `setDefaultThinkingLevel`, packages/shared/src/config/storage.ts:2495-2502), so there is nothing to hold and nothing to release, and a switch to Fable 5 / Opus 4.8 / Opus 4.7 silently carries the previous model's level over.  One structural consequence for the fix: `:506` puts the model default BELOW the configured level, but our chain terminates at `getDefaultThinkingLevel()`, which always returns a concrete value. A model default inserted underneath it would be dead code unless the shipped config default is made distinguishable from a real user choice.

column8: None observable. Today the Nessy Gateway answers `/api/v1/cli/models` directly, so the model picker fills normally and no user sees a difference either way. It surfaces the moment something in front of that path answers with a 3xx — a gateway misconfiguration, an ops-side path move, or a TLS-terminating corporate proxy that redirects to a login host: at startup and on every Nessy Gateway auth/refresh the app would silently hand the user's `Nestor-Token` JWT to whatever host the 30x names, with no dialog, no toast and no log line naming the new host (index.ts:96 logs only a model count). column8: Narrow but real, and silent when it bites — on the default Pi runtime, today.  A user writes (or installs a Claude plugin that ships) a `PreToolUse`/`PostToolUse`/`Stop`/`SubagentStop` hook that branches on effort — the documented use is exactly that, e.g. requiring approval for expensive tools only at low effort, or tagging an audit log with the level the turn actually ran at. Both documented ways of reading it come back empty: `jq -r '.effort.level'` over the stdin payload yields `null`, and `echo "$CLAUDE_EFFORT"` inside the hook prints nothing. The hook does not error and does not warn — it takes the unset branch, so a policy hook meant to tighten at low effort silently never tightens. Same for a Bash tool call: `echo $CLAUDE_EFFORT` in any command the model runs prints empty.  This is not surfaced anywhere. Unlike the ConfigChange matcher case there is no `matcher_never_matches`-style registration diagnostic for a missing input field, so nothing tells the hook author the field will always be absent.  One partial exception, unverified and off by default: on the Claude backend (`NESSY_FEATURE_PROVIDER_CLAUDE`), a plugin hook's stdin JSON is the SDK's own input object spread verbatim (hooks-automation.ts:1643-1646), so `effort.level` may already arrive there. `$CLAUDE_EFFORT` is still never set on that path, because the env builder mirrors a closed field list.

column8: None observable for anyone on the default. The cap is 8 in both products, so behaviour is identical unless a user deliberately reaches for the documented knob.  It surfaces the moment someone follows hooks-guide.md § *Stop hook hits the block cap* — which is exactly the audience that hits it, since the doc prescribes the variable as the remedy for a hook that legitimately needs more than eight iterations. That user exports `CLAUDE_CODE_STOP_HOOK_BLOCK_CAP=20`, restarts Nessy, and nothing changes: from the 9th consecutive block onward their Stop (or SubagentStop) hook's `reason` silently stops reaching the model, so the agent stops being told what still needs doing and the convergence loop the hook was driving stalls one iteration short. There is no UI signal at all — the suppression writes only `this.debug(...)` (packages/shared/src/agent/base-agent.ts:565), which lands in logs, not in the chat surface, so the symptom the user sees is "my hook stopped having any effect" with no explanation. `0` (disable the cap) is equally inert.  Note the fork's cap suppresses re-delivery of the reason rather than force-ending a continued turn (deliberate — packages/shared/src/agent/base-agent.ts:550-553; we cannot re-run a finished turn), so the symptom differs in shape from Claude's "turn ends with a warning", but the trigger point and the missing knob are the same.

column8: Latent-but-reachable, and silent when it bites. Today: install any Claude plugin whose `PreToolUse`/`PostToolUse`/`Stop`/`SubagentStop` hook branches on effort — the common shape is `level=$(jq -r '.effort.level')` or `[ "$CLAUDE_EFFORT" = low ]` to skip an expensive check on cheap turns — and the hook reads `null`/empty and takes the wrong branch. It exits 0, so nothing is logged, no hook-error notice appears in the session, and the user sees only that the plugin "does not seem to do anything": an expensive gate that was meant to be skipped runs on every turn, or a guard that was meant to fire never does. Same for a Bash tool call inside a turn: `echo $CLAUDE_EFFORT` prints a blank line. The asymmetry makes it more surprising, not less — the same documented variable DOES expand inside a skill body (packages/shared/src/capabilities/runtime-skill-content.ts:136), so a user who verified it in a skill will reasonably assume it works in the hook and the shell too. Nothing surfaces it except reading the hook's own output; no first-party Nessy surface depends on it.

column8: Today, concretely: a user installs a Claude plugin whose `hooks/hooks.json` declares a `DirectoryAdded` hook (the doc's own example is "Install dependencies for a repository added mid-session"). The install succeeds, that hook is dropped from the plugin's capabilities, and the install result carries a warning reading `External hook event "DirectoryAdded" is not mapped for claude compatibility.` — which reads as a typo in the plugin rather than a known Nessy gap, unlike `MessageDisplay`/`TeammateIdle` which import as recorded deferrals. The Sources UI does not render plugin diagnostics today, so inside the desktop app the visible outcome is just a hook silently missing from the plugin's capability list; the wording is visible through the marketplace/install RPC response and the agent-facing plugin-management tool result. A user hand-writing `DirectoryAdded` into a hooks config file gets the load error `<source>: DirectoryAdded is not an agent lifecycle hook event`. Beyond the wording, nothing the plugin author wrote would run even if the name were accepted: the fork has no `/add-dir` command and no `register_repo_root` control request, so the only way a working directory is added mid-session is another hook granting `updatedPermissions.addDirectories` at session scope — a path that fires no event at all. What would make the full gap surface is shipping a user-facing add-directory action; until then, the observable part of this is the misclassified install warning.

column8: Concrete and silent. A user installs a Claude plugin (or writes a hook) whose SessionStart/Setup/CwdChanged/FileChanged script follows the documented recipe — `if [ -n "$CLAUDE_ENV_FILE" ]; then echo 'export NODE_ENV=production' >> "$CLAUDE_ENV_FILE"; fi`, or the `nvm use 20` / venv / direnv variant. On Nessy the variable is unset, the guard is false, the hook exits 0, and it does literally nothing: no error notice, no transcript entry, nothing in the hook error surface. The user then watches every Bash tool call run without the environment their setup hook was supposed to establish — wrong Node or Python version, missing `./node_modules/.bin` on PATH, missing project env — and the agent reports a toolchain mismatch with no pointer to the cause. The un-guarded variant is worse in a different way: `>> "$CLAUDE_ENV_FILE"` on an empty path fails, the hook exits non-zero, and the user gets a bare `<hook name> hook error` notice with no explanation of why. Nothing surfaces the real reason on either shape today.

column8: An administrator who follows settings.md and writes `"autoUpdate": true` on an `extraKnownMarketplaces` entry in managed settings gets silence: the key is dropped at parse with no drop record and no doctor warning, so the policy looks accepted. The marketplace is still registered, but its catalog only refreshes when a user opens the marketplace browse surface, or clicks Upgrade on that registry by hand. The installed plugins from it never update: the plugin row's Update action is permanently unavailable because `canUpdate` is hard-false, so a user cannot even see that a newer version exists. Concretely, a fleet pinned to an internal marketplace stays on whatever plugin version was installed on day one, indefinitely, and both the administrator and the user believe otherwise.

column5: The entire mechanism is absent, not misnamed and not narrowed. Six separable pieces are each missing: the per-marketplace `autoUpdate` boolean (unparsed from managed policy, unpersisted on the registry row, unexposed on the wire, absent from the UI); the polarity-dependent default (official-Anthropic-on / third-party-and-local-off — the fork has no concept of an 'official Anthropic marketplace' at all, so even the discriminator is missing); the post-startup check with a randomized delay of up to ten minutes; the installed-bundle update itself (`update()` is a pure alias of `repair()` — same-version re-stage, never a version comparison); the `/reload-plugins`-equivalent notification after an update lands; and both env kill-switches. The one adjacent behaviour that DOES exist — `ensureBackgroundFetch` re-cloning a stale catalog off the request path — is browse-triggered rather than scheduled and updates catalog metadata only, so it is not a narrower version of the documented behaviour but a different one. Because nothing ever sets `availableUpdateVersion`, even the manual path never tells a user an update exists.

column8: Concrete and observable, in two places. A user who installs a plugin from a marketplace never learns a newer version exists: the plugin row's Update action is permanently unavailable because `canUpdate` is computed from a field nothing ever writes (views.ts:443 over resolver input storage-runtime.ts:826), so the only way to get a new version is to notice by hand, click the per-registry Upgrade button on the Plugins page to re-clone the catalog, then click the plugin's Repair — and the repair path re-stages the same version anyway unless the catalog moved. Plugins therefore sit at their install-time version indefinitely, including through upstream security fixes. Second, an administrator who writes `"autoUpdate": true` on an `extraKnownMarketplaces` entry from Claude's page gets nothing and is told nothing: the key is dropped before the managed-policy drop sink sees it, so it appears in neither config-doctor output nor the managed-drop report, and the marketplace behaves exactly as if the key were absent. There is no auto-update toggle anywhere in the plugin manager UI, so a user following the documented four-step path finds no such control.

(b) Tag-based version selection: nothing lists `{plugin-name}--v{version}` tags, so `version` can only ever be an after-the-fact verdict on an already-present install, never a selector for which version to fetch. Net effect on a declared `~2.1.0`: it can disable a plugin but can never satisfy one. Four page behaviours fall out of the same root: range intersection across dependents and its install-time `range-conflict` (:142-:148), the cross-marketplace refusal and `allowCrossMarketplaceDependenciesOn` (:81, :104), `--prune` of orphaned auto-installed dependencies and the provenance bit it needs (:180-:198), and the `no-matching-tag` error (:215).

column8: None observable against the official Claude catalogue today. Measured 2026-08-02: 0 of the 276 entries in `anthropics/claude-plugins-official`'s `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json` carry a `dependencies` key (the union of entry keys is author/category/description/displayName/homepage/keywords/lspServers/name/skills/source/strict/tags/version), and 0 of the 74 per-plugin `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` manifests fetched at their pinned shas from the 81 git-subdir/github entries declare one. It surfaces the first time a team points Nessy at an internal marketplace that uses the documented bundle pattern (:52-:70): the user runs one install of `backend-standard`, Sources shows it installed, and it does nothing — because its manifest is only a `dependencies` array, none of its four plugins is present, `resolveActiveDependencyErrors` marks it `dependency-unsatisfied`, and resolver.ts:1703-1707 disables every capability it has. The visible text is dependencies.ts:151, "This plugin requires <name>, which is not installed or is disabled. Install it, or enable it if it is already installed.", repeated per dependency, and the same list appears under `errors` in `nessy-general-agent plugin list --json`. A constrained dependency behaves the same even when the user installs it by hand: if the version they happen to get is outside the range they get `dependency-version-unsatisfied` (dependencies.ts:122-131) with no way for Nessy to fetch the matching tag. The workaround — install each dependency manually, which :104 itself blesses — works; what is missing is the one-install-for-a-curated-set promise the page is written around.

column5: The whole mechanism is absent; only the file's existence is noticed. Nothing parses `settings.json`, so neither documented key is read, and no value is applied. Four deltas, separable: (a) `agent` — the fork has no main-thread-agent override to route it into, so this is not a wrong key name or a narrowed value, it is a missing capability class; the nearest existing seam is the child-only `childSystemPrompt` append at pi-agent.ts:6615 and the app-level `outputStyleId` knob at config/storage.ts:57, and neither has a main-thread agent analogue. (b) `subagentStatusLine` — zero source hits repo-wide; the whole statusline surface is separately absent and is owned by f206. (c) The priority rule (`settings.json` outranks `plugin.json`'s `settings`) is unrepresentable, not just unapplied: the externalKind dedupe at claude.ts:2299 emits one row for both spellings. (d) "Unknown keys are silently ignored" is trivially satisfied for the wrong reason — every key is ignored, known ones included. One thing that is NOT a delta and must not be re-fixed: the detection itself is correct and its `deferred` record is the right shape; what is missing beside it is the `refusal` diagnostic that the `themes` row at claude.ts:2247-2252 already demonstrates. column8: Two things, one silent and one not. Silent: a user installs a Claude plugin whose whole point is to change the default behaviour — the doc's own example is a `security-reviewer` plugin — clicks Install on the Plugins page, gets a green 'installed' toast, and the agent never activates. Nothing in the app says so, and nothing says so to the plugin author either: the deferred row exists but the only code path that renders `plugins.compatDeferredEntry` is the blocked-install message at PluginsPage.tsx:1851-1859. Not silent, and arguably worse: because the file's mere presence forces `compatibility.state: 'partial'` (claude.ts:484), the FIRST time that user clicks Update or Repair on that plugin, `repairUnlocked` purges its activation grants (management-service-v2.ts:553-554), the plugin switches off, and the card shows a 'Confirm enable' shield button (PluginsPage.tsx:1476-1481) with no stated reason — the user sees a working plugin spontaneously disable itself after an update. That happens to any Claude bundle carrying a plugin-root `settings.json`, whatever it contains, including one whose keys we would ignore anyway.

column5: The whole mechanism is missing, not a key name or a value. Three separable deltas. (a) Discovery: no scanner ever stats `<skills-dir>/<name>/.claude-plugin/plugin.json`; `skillRecords` gates on `SKILL.md` alone (`native-sources.ts:282`), so a doc-conformant bundle — which per `:383` puts its skills at `<folder>/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` and need carry no root `SKILL.md` — contributes NOTHING. Only the subset that happens to also carry a root `SKILL.md` degrades to a bare skill with its agents/hooks/MCP silently dropped; the filed prose asserted that degraded case universally, which overstates one shape and understates the other. (b) Loading model: the doc's plugin is discovered in place and never enters the cache (`:376`), and has no uninstall because nothing was installed (`:409`); our only representation of a plugin is a cache-resident `PluginInstalledEntryV2` with a required `cacheRef` (`store-v2.ts:48`) placed by `install()` (`store-v2.ts:198`-`:200`). (c) Identity and control: `skills-dir` exists in neither `PluginOriginSource` (`plugins/types.ts:35`) nor the managed marketplace-source classifier (`managed-marketplace-entries.ts:170`-`:206`), so the key `<name>@skills-dir` cannot be produced and the documented `{"source": "skills-dir"}` admin switch is parsed as invalid and dropped. Also missing but subordinate: `/reload-plugins`, `plugin init`, and a `plugin disable` verb. Note the two roots the doc names (`~/.claude/skills/`, `<cwd>/.claude/skills/`) are not scanned at all in the fork under any name — the equivalent roots we do scan are `~/.agents/skills` and `<cwd>/.agents/skills` — so this is not a rebrand-path difference: the mechanism is absent whatever the directory is called.

column7: `buildNativeCapabilityInventory` has exactly ONE production caller, `buildCapabilityResolutionInputsV2` (`packages/server-core/src/bootstrap/storage-runtime.ts:635`), whose output is the `CapabilityResolutionInputs` snapshot behind every agent turn's pinned capability context (`packages/shared/src/agent/base-agent.ts:95` imports the module). Direct test coverage of the inventory: `packages/shared/src/capabilities/__tests__/native-sources.test.ts`, `rules-tier.test.ts`, `nested-instruction-discovery.test.ts`. Other readers of the inventory shape: `packages/shared/src/capabilities/invalidation.ts:24`, `packages/shared/src/capabilities/resolver.ts`, `packages/shared/src/capabilities/project-contribution-detect.ts:21`. On the plugin side, `resolvePluginProjectionCandidates` (`packages/shared/src/plugins/projection-candidates.ts:139`) and `packages/shared/src/capabilities/materializer.ts` gain entries whose bundle root is outside the plugin cache — covered by `packages/server-core/src/sessions/__tests__/plugin-capability-runtime.test.ts`, `packages/shared/src/plugins/__tests__/store-v2.test.ts`, `management-service-v2.test.ts`. THREE boundaries are crossed and each is a risk trigger in this repo. (1) PERSISTENCE: if the ephemeral-entry route is abandoned in favour of registry rows, `PluginInstalledRegistryV2` (`store-v2.ts:63`, `schemaVersion: 2`) needs `cacheRef` to become optional — `readInstalledRegistry` (`store-v2.ts:161`) throws "Incompatible plugin registry schema; refusing to import" on any bump, so a version change is a hard migration. The recommended change avoids this; verify it stays avoided. (2) MANAGED POLICY / SECURITY: `managed-marketplace-entries.ts` is an org allowlist whose documented polarity is fail-closed (`settings.md:194`, quoted at `managed-marketplace-entries.test.ts:71`); a wrong arm silently widens what an org allows. (3) TRUST + WIRE: project-scope roots must stay behind `projectTrustState === 'trusted'` (`native-sources.ts:995`) and their MCP servers behind the existing per-server approval (`:395`); and if the UI is to show `<name>@skills-dir` provenance, the generated protocol types `packages/codex-protocol/generated/v2/PluginDetail.ts` and `SkillsListEntry.ts` change with it. Adding `'skills-dir'` to `PluginOriginSource` (`plugins/types.ts:35`) fans out to every exhaustive switch over the union across `packages/shared/src/plugins` and `packages/shared/src/marketplace`.
column8: A user who follows Claude's own docs and drops a plugin folder into a skills directory gets total silence. Concretely: create `~/.agents/skills/my-tool/.claude-plugin/plugin.json` (or the doc-literal `~/.claude/skills/my-tool/...`) with bundled `agents/`, `hooks/` and `.mcp.json`, restart the app, and nothing appears anywhere — the Skills panel shows no `my-tool`, the plugin list shows no `my-tool@skills-dir`, the bundled agents/hooks/MCP servers/output styles never load, and no diagnostic is emitted, because `skillRecords` (`native-sources.ts:282`) simply `continue`s past a folder with no root `SKILL.md`. The only partially-visible variant is a bundle that also carries a root `SKILL.md`: then the skill text loads as a plain skill and every other component is dropped without a word. There is no error to search for, so the failure reads as "the app ignored my file". Secondary, latent: an org that ships `{"source": "skills-dir"}` in managed `blockedMarketplaces` gets a dropped-entry diagnostic instead of an enforced control (`managed-marketplace-entries.test.ts:56`) — harmless while the scan does not exist, but it will read as "policy applied" the moment it does, so the policy arm must land in the same change as the scan, not after it.

column5: Two separate absences, both real, neither a renamed key or a wrong value. (a) SESSION SCOPE — the whole mechanism is missing, not narrowed. Nothing in this fork can load a plugin for one session and forget it: `PluginScope` (`plugins/types.ts:4`) has three persistent members and the capability assembly (`storage-runtime.ts:729`) accepts only committed `PluginInstalledEntryV2[]`. The nearest shipped behaviour — install from a URL or local path — is the opposite of the documented one: it writes an installed record, so it violates plugins/cli-reference.md#flags-that-load-a-plugin-for-one-session (was line 1096 of the retired plugins-reference page) ("no installed record") and plugins.md:344 ("that session only"), and it offers no name-override-for-this-session semantics (plugins.md:328). (b) ARCHIVE FORMAT — present but for the wrong format. We have a hardened zip extractor (`mcpb-archive.ts:37-150`) and we refuse to point it at a plugin bundle: the gates at `install-service.ts:569-570`/`:805-806` require an MCPB root `manifest.json`, so a `.zip` of a plugin directory is either stored as an opaque file or handed to a tar extractor. That half is genuinely `built-partial` inside an otherwise `not-built` feature. Note also which flag is unimplementable-as-written and which is not: `--plugin-dir` is a Claude Code CLI flag and our product's primary surface is the Electron app, so the faithful equivalent is a session-scoped side-load input on the session-create boundary plus the CLI flags for `apps/cli`; the archive-format half has a direct, surface-independent fix.

column8: Two concrete failures today. (1) A plugin author cannot try a plugin without installing it. There is no equivalent of `claude --plugin-dir ./my-plugin`: the only way in is Plugins → install, which commits an entry to the plugin registry and an activation record, so testing an iteration means install → test → uninstall, and a local copy can never temporarily shadow the same plugin already installed from a marketplace (plugins.md:328). (2) A plugin shipped as a `.zip` cannot be installed at all, by any route. In the desktop app the native picker (Create ▾ → import) is filtered to `.mcpb`/`.dxt` (`apps/electron/src/preload/mcpb-import.ts:17`), so `my-plugin.zip` is not even selectable; forcing it through returns the toast `plugins.mcpbUnsupported` with detail `marketplace.mcpb.invalid_archive`. Reaching the same file through the install-source resolver instead stages the zip as an opaque file and the install fails with `plugin.format.unsupported_format`. A zip hosted at a URL — the doc's stated use case, 'a CI build artifact' (plugins.md:344) — reaches the tar-only extractor and dies with `plugin.install.archive_fetch_failed`. Only an MCPB extension (root `manifest.json`, `manifest_version` 0.1–0.3) unpacks. The name collision makes this worse than a plain gap: a `.zip` that happens to be an MCPB bundle installs fine, so the failure looks arbitrary from the outside.

column8: Concrete and silent. Many MCP servers document their own JSON as `"type": "streamable-http"`, because that is the MCP specification's name for the transport. A user who pastes that block into `.mcp.json`, `~/.nessy/mcp.json` or `.nessy-agent/mcp.json` gets a server that never connects and exposes no tools. It is not simply missing from the UI: the capability inventory keys off the server name regardless of `type` (native-sources.ts:493-503), and with `transport` unset but `url` present the panel labels it `http` via the fallback at resolver.ts:1653 — so the MCP/Sources surface lists an apparently-normal HTTP server that produces nothing. The only trace is `Ignoring .mcp.json server "<name>": unsupported MCP server config`, routed to a `debug` callback that defaults to a no-op (runtime-pool-servers.ts:273), so with no debug sink attached there is no message at all. The user's next move is to suspect their token or the server. Same for plugin install: a Claude plugin bundling a `.mcp.json` with that spelling imports with the server missing and the diagnostic `Claude MCP server requires a command (stdio) or url (http/sse/ws).`, which is misleading — the entry does have a `url`.

column8: Observable today, on the two-way path. With `channelsEnabled` on and a channel source pushing during a live turn, the event body is injected as if the user had typed it mid-turn: no source, no attributes. A user running a chat-bridge channel (the page's own webhook example) sees the model unable to route a reply — the `chat_id` it is told to pass back never appears in its context, so it either omits the argument, invents one, or asks the user which conversation this was; with two channel sources armed on one session the model cannot say which one fired, and can attribute an alert to the wrong system. For a one-way alert channel the effect is milder but still visible: the alert reads as a user instruction, so the model tends to act on it as a new task rather than as an event to note. Latent half: nothing surfaces at all while a session is idle, because that push is dropped before this code runs (f134).

column5: The entire client-side roots surface is missing — this is not a wrong key name or a narrowed value. Three distinct absences: the `roots` client capability (with `listChanged: true`) is never declared at the MCP handshake; no `roots/list` request handler is registered, so the method does not exist on our client; `notifications/roots/list_changed` is never emitted. The data the doc says to answer with is already computed and correct in this repo (workspace root + `additionalDirectories` + session `addDirectories` grants) — it simply has no path to the MCP wire. Secondary structural delta: Claude Code has one MCP client per session, so its roots are per-session; Nessy's pool is shared per (workspaceId, projectKey) and leased by sessions (workspace-mcp-pool-registry.ts:165-166, :201-230), so one connection cannot answer differently per session — a decision the implementation must make explicitly rather than inherit.

column7: CROSSES A WIRE BOUNDARY — a risk trigger in this repo. The client `capabilities` object is sent in the MCP `initialize` handshake to every third-party server on every transport (stdio, http, sse, ws — client.ts:371-425), so this changes what every connected server sees at connect time, adds a new inbound request method (`roots/list`) and a new outbound notification. It also crosses a data-egress boundary that did not exist before: `roots/list` discloses absolute local filesystem paths to every connected server, including REMOTE http/sse/ws servers that previously received none. Callers and readers: packages/shared/src/mcp/mcp-pool.ts:1136 is the sole production constructor of `NessyMcpClient`; the `PoolClient` interface (client.ts:234-255) is implemented by `ApiSourcePoolClient` (api-source-pool-client.ts:15) and consumed throughout the pool, so the new member must stay optional; packages/server-core/src/mcp/workspace-mcp-pool-registry.ts:789 is the sole production pool factory, and the pool is keyed per (workspaceId, projectKey) and shared across session leases (:165-166, :201-230). Downstream of the pool, packages/shared/src/mcp/pool-server.ts:210-213 re-exposes the pool to Pi and Codex as `nessy-pool-proxy`; it is a server, not a client, so it is unaffected unless a later change forwards roots through it. Tests that pin the touched surfaces: packages/shared/src/mcp/__tests__/client-transport.test.ts:65-120 (capabilities and handler registry), and the pool suites under packages/shared/src/mcp/__tests__/ (proxy-tool-names.test.ts, runtime-pool-servers.test.ts) construct raw SDK clients and pools. No persistence boundary is crossed: the roots answer is derived at request time from `workspaceRootPath` plus the already-persisted `additionalDirectories`; nothing new is written to disk. Imported-plugin path: plugin-provided MCP servers connect through the same pool (`pluginRuntime` branch at client.ts:373-380), so they gain roots along with native and project servers.
column8: Latent for most users today, and concretely broken for one class of server. A user connects an MCP server that scopes its own filesystem access via roots (the pattern mcp.md:108 explicitly routes servers to): the server's `initialize` response shows a client with no `roots` capability, so it never asks, falls back to its own default — typically nothing, or an operator-configured allowlist — and its file tools then either refuse ('no accessible roots' / 'path not allowed') or operate on the wrong directory. In the Sources surface such a server connects and lists tools normally, so nothing looks wrong; the failure appears only when a tool is called. Second, invisible-by-construction effect: a user who adds a working directory mid-session (the `addDirectories` grant path, pi-agent.ts:3193) or edits `additionalDirectories` in settings gets no `notifications/roots/list_changed`, so even a server that had roots would keep the stale set for the life of the connection. What would make it surface broadly: any commonly installed server adopting roots-based scoping — the mechanism is client-advertised, so adoption on the server side alone turns this from latent into a visible tool failure with no diagnostic pointing at us.

column5: The entire mechanism is absent — this is not a key-name or a value mismatch. Claude runs a shell command at each connect and merges its stdout JSON over the static headers; we parse the field off the config and connect with static headers only. Four separable deltas: (a) no executor at all — no spawn, no 10s timeout, no stdout JSON contract, no dynamic-over-static merge; (b) no helper environment — `CLAUDE_CODE_MCP_SERVER_NAME`/`CLAUDE_CODE_MCP_SERVER_URL`/`CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT` exist nowhere in code, and there is no plugin-root cwd rule; (c) no 401/403 re-run-and-retry-once; (d) the reporting we do have is itself asymmetric — the plugin path warns and files a deferred record on every transport, the `.mcp.json` path warns only on `ws`, and on `http`/`sse` (the two transports the doc's own examples use) the field is dropped in total silence, which is exactly the failure mode the code comment at project-config.ts:141-143 says the warning exists to prevent.
