column7: `SdkMcpServerConfig` is the shared MCP config type: it is read by `sdkConfigToClientConfig` and `mcpConnectionKey` (packages/shared/src/mcp/mcp-pool.ts:429, :160 — the sha256 connection identity, so any field added to it changes identity for servers that declare it), `BaseAgent.syncSources` (packages/shared/src/agent/base-agent.ts:1698, :1731-1800), pi-agent.ts:7014, claude-agent.ts, runtime-pool-servers.ts, plugins/runtime-projection.ts:92 `buildPluginMcpServerConfig`, and mcp/builtin-dp-servers.ts:214. The MCP pool lives in the HOST process (base-agent syncs it directly), so no Pi/Claude subprocess wire is crossed by the connection itself. Two boundaries ARE crossed and both are risk triggers in this repo. PERSISTENCE: `PluginMcpDescriptor` is part of `NessyPluginManifest`, which is persisted per install in the plugin registry on disk (packages/shared/src/plugins/store-v2.ts:42-69) — plugins installed before the change carry a manifest without the field until re-normalized, which is what the `CLAUDE_ADAPTER_VERSION` bump plus `migrateOutdatedPluginAdaptersOnStartup` (packages/shared/src/plugins/adapter-migration.ts:17-56) exists to drive. TRUST: a plugin MCP capability's `executableHash` is sha256 over the bundle hash and `JSON.stringify({definition,…})` (packages/shared/src/plugins/projection-candidates.ts:84-90), so once a declaring plugin's normalized descriptor gains `headersHelper`, its per-capability trust grant no longer matches and the user is asked to re-grant — for that plugin only; a plugin that declares no helper hashes byte-identically. SECURITY: this introduces a NEW arbitrary-shell-execution path at connect time. For project scope the doc's precondition is already satisfied structurally — `.mcp.json` is only read inside the `projectTrustState === 'trusted'` branch (packages/shared/src/capabilities/native-sources.ts:995, :1067) — but that must be re-verified, not assumed, and the helper must never inherit a path that lets an untrusted project contribute one. Tests that currently assert the ABSENCE and will fail loudly: packages/shared/src/mcp/__tests__/ws-transport.test.ts:46-57, packages/shared/src/plugins/__tests__/claude-mcp-ws.test.ts:82-96, packages/shared/src/plugins/__tests__/user-config-substitution.test.ts:197-213. The deferred reason code `plugin.deferred.claude_mcp_headers_helper_unsupported` reaches the renderer at install time (packages/server-core/src/handlers/rpc/plugins.ts:155, apps/electron/src/renderer/pages/plugin-install-state.ts:19-45, PluginsPage.tsx:294) — removing it changes what that surface shows.
column8: An operator whose internal MCP server authenticates with Kerberos, an SSO cookie or a short-lived token — the doc's stated audience, and the normal corporate-gateway case in this fork — configures `headersHelper` and the server simply never works. Concretely: put a `.mcp.json` with `{"type":"http","url":…,"headersHelper":"/opt/bin/get-mcp-auth-headers.sh"}` in a trusted project and open a session; the helper is never executed, the connection goes out with whatever static headers exist (usually none), the server 401s, its tools never appear in the session, and NOTHING is said — no toast, no diagnostic, not even a warning line, because the http/sse arm drops the field silently and the ws arm's warning only reaches the agent debug log. The user sees a server that is configured and absent. On the imported-Claude-plugin path the outcome is the same, but there the user does get a signal: the plugin's install result lists a deferred `mcp` capability with reason `plugin.deferred.claude_mcp_headers_helper_unsupported`, so at least the cause is nameable. A `ws` server declaring it is worse still — the WebSocket transport sends no headers at all (packages/shared/src/mcp/client.ts:416), so neither the static nor the dynamic set arrives.

column8: Observable, and worst for installed plugins. A user runs a skill written for Claude Code with `context: fork` — say a research or PR-summary skill whose whole point is a throwaway context — and instead of a background subagent returning a summary, the entire SKILL.md is spliced into the live conversation and executed there: full history visible to the task (the opposite of what the skill's prompt assumes), the main context window consumed by the skill's own work, no separate background completion message, and no way to keep working while it runs. Nothing at invocation time says so. The author-facing warning added by 55b711ce is reachable only through an explicit `skill_validate` call (packages/session-tools-core/src/handlers/skill-validate.ts:116-129) or the config-doctor aggregate (packages/shared/src/config/validators.ts:487); the write-time gate at packages/shared/src/agent/core/pre-tool-use.ts:509-517 acts on `!validationResult.valid` only, so warnings are dropped when a SKILL.md is written through a tool. One direction where we are safer, not worse: skills.md:559 warns that a backgrounded fork's edits escape `/rewind`; ours run inside the session and stay checkpointed.

column8: Concrete and reachable today. In a monorepo session opened at the repo root, a skill that a package owns — `apps/web/.agents/skills/deploy/SKILL.md` or `apps/web/.nessy-agent/skills/deploy/SKILL.md` — never becomes available, no matter how many files under `apps/web` the agent reads or edits. It is absent from the `<available_skills>` block the model sees (prompt-builder.ts:403), absent from the `/` command menu (SessionManager.ts:16038), and typing `/deploy` or `[skill:deploy]` resolves to nothing or to the root variant. The user's only options are to reopen the session with its working directory inside `apps/web`, or to move the skill to the project root and gate it with `paths:`. Second, smaller surface, present even without nested support: when two skills DO share a slug across the ancestor layers, the losing one is dropped from the `/` menu entirely (custom-commands.ts:444) rather than offered under a qualified name — the user sees one `/deploy` and has no way to reach the other except by typing the internal capability key `[skill:skill::project::<workspaceId>::<projectKey>::d1::deploy]`, which is neither documented nor shown anywhere in the UI.

(c) EFFECT — the two functions that would do the work (`clearSessionMessages`, storage.ts:457; `clearHistory`, base-agent.ts:1605 and the three overrides) have zero production callers. Note the fix is NOT "add 'clear' to SDK_SLASH_COMMANDS": per slash-commands.md:214 an SDK-dispatched `/clear` inside our per-turn one-shot `query()` is not what produces empty context — dropping the `resume:` anchor (`this.sessionId = null`, already implemented in ClaudeAgent.clearHistory at :2745) is. column5: The entire mechanism is absent, not misnamed and not narrowed: no `/btw` command id, no parser, no non-persisting answer channel, no ephemeral overlay, no earlier-answers list, no fork-from-overlay. Two of the doc's four ingredients do have substrate — a tool-less single-response model call (`queryLlm`) and an in-memory transcript to feed it (`managed.messages`) — but they are not connected, and the one path that connects a user's text to a model today is the path that writes history. So the missing piece is specifically a send route that reads the transcript, answers once with no tools, and never touches `managed.messages`/`persistSession`, plus a renderer overlay to hold the answer. Two sub-behaviours are additionally unbuildable on today's primitives without extra work: prompt-cache reuse of the parent conversation (our `queryLlm` runs an ephemeral Pi session with no history) and the `f` fork into a new session inheriting the parent transcript plus the Q/A as real turns.

column8: Observable and immediate. A user who follows the Claude Code guidance and types `/btw what was that config file again?` gets no `btw` entry in the inline `/` menu (apps/electron/src/renderer/components/ui/slash-command-menu.tsx:225-239), so the line submits as an ordinary prompt: it is appended to the transcript (SessionManager.ts:15261-15269), flushed to the session file on disk (:15276-15278), rendered as a normal user bubble, and the answer is a full tool-enabled turn that grows the context window — the exact opposite of "never enters conversation history … without growing context". If the agent is mid-turn it is worse than useless: the send is steered into the in-flight turn or queued behind it (SessionManager.ts:15155+), i.e. it derails the long-running task the doc says a side question must not interrupt. On a first message it also becomes the session title source (:15294-15320). So today the only way to ask a throwaway question is to pay for it in context, in the transcript, and possibly in the running turn.

column8: Concrete and immediate. There is also no automatic recap when the user returns to an idle session. Separately observable: typing `:heart:` inserts the literal characters (no emoji), and after `! npm test` the command output lands in the transcript but Claude does not respond to it, so the user must send a second prompt to get the failure explained — Claude Code has responded automatically since v2.1.186. Not observable: `editorMode`/`vimInsertModeRemaps`, which would need a composer-side editor mode to have any surface at all.

column5: The whole mechanism is missing, not a renamed field: no `/heapdump` command on any surface (desktop slash menu, CLI, agent-callable allowlist), no V8 snapshot writer, no `-diagnostics.json` breakdown, and no `~/Desktop`/home output path. Two secondary deltas matter for the fix. (a) Shape: the only memory data we produce is `ServerStatus.memory = { heapUsed, heapTotal, rss }` (packages/core/src/types/server.ts:25-29) — three counters delivered over RPC to a caller that never displays them, where the doc requires four buckets (resident set size, JS heap, array buffers, unaccounted native memory) persisted to a file; `arrayBuffers`/`external` are not even sampled, so the JS-versus-native discrimination the doc says the breakdown exists for is impossible today. (b) Process topology: Claude Code dumps the single CLI process, while here the memory can grow in the Electron main (which hosts SessionManager and the Pi client in-process) or in the Pi agent subprocess, so a faithful implementation has to name which process each artifact came from — a decision the page does not make for us.

column8: Today a user whose Nessy Desktop climbs into the gigabytes has no way to produce a shareable artifact. The `/` menu shows fourteen feature commands and none concerns process memory (`/memory` opens session MEMORY.md); `nessy-general-agent --help` lists no memory command and `doctor` reports configuration only; the Debug menu that could host one is compiled out of packaged builds (apps/electron/src/main/menu.ts:193 `!app.isPackaged`). The three counters we do compute (`server:getStatus`) are never rendered — the Settings server page reads the unrelated `settings:getServerStatus` — so even the numbers are invisible. Practical consequence: a memory report from a real user can only say 'it got slow', and nobody can tell JS-heap growth from native growth, or tell the Electron main apart from the Pi subprocess. Nothing breaks until someone tries to diagnose a leak; the moment they do, the documented recovery step simply does not exist.

column8: None observable today, in either direction. A user cannot express the intent — there is no `--agent` flag, no `--agents` flag and no `agent` setting, so no agent definition ever runs as the main session and there is no turn for an `initialPrompt` to be submitted into. And a user who writes `initialPrompt:` in `~/.nessy-agent/agents/<name>.md`, or installs a Claude plugin whose agent file carries it, sees nothing at all: the key is silently discarded by both frontmatter readers, the agent still loads and runs normally, and no error, warning or doctor line names the ignored field. It surfaces the moment a main-session-agent surface ships (the field would then be the only part still missing), or as a support question the first time someone ports a Claude agent that relies on the auto-submitted turn and gets an empty session instead — with nothing on screen to explain why.

column8: Concrete and bad on the most common setup. In the Desktop app, from a session in the DEFAULT permission mode (the shipped default), launch a workflow — the `ultracode`/keyword route, the `workflow` tool, or a saved `/<name>` — and approve the launch card. From then on every single file edit by every spawned agent raises its own approval modal in the main session (`file_write`, pre-tool-use.ts:1944-1949, routed out of the hidden child by permissionSurfaceRouting), each agent blocking until it is answered, for a run the page presents as an unattended background fan-out in the Background tasks pane. A ten-agent workflow that touches three files each is thirty modals; unanswered children sit until the spawn deadline (spawner.ts:607, default 30 min) and the run then reports errors. The user's only workaround today is to switch the session to acceptEdits or auto BEFORE launching — which the doc explicitly says should not be necessary. Latent ("none observable") for sessions already in acceptEdits, auto or bypassPermissions, and for `claude -p`-equivalent headless runs which the page exempts anyway.

column5: The entire mechanism is missing — not a wrong key name, not a narrower match. column6: packages/server-core/src/pi-harness/worktree-include-plan.ts (parseWorktreeInclude, worktreeIncludeCandidateCommands, worktreeIncludePlan (new file)) — New pure planner, sibling to worktree-git-plan.ts and following the same 'assertable without a repository' shape. (1) `parseWorktreeInclude(text: string): WorktreeIncludePattern[]` — gitignore syntax: drop blank lines and `#` comments (`\#` escapes), trim unescaped trailing whitespace, record `negated` for a leading `!`, `anchored` for a leading `/`, `directoryOnly` for a trailing `/`. Cap entries (reuse the 128/512 limits from worktree-settings.ts) and refuse `..` segments and absolute forms exactly as `repoRelativePaths` does — a `.worktreeinclude` must not be able to name a file outside the repo. (2) `worktreeIncludeCandidateCommands(repoRoot)` → the `WorktreeGitCommand`s that produce the authoritative candidate set: `['-C', repoRoot, 'ls-files', '-z', '--others', '--ignored', '--exclude-standard', '--directory', '--no-empty-directory']` (operation `include-list`, cwd `repo`, `allowFailure: true`) — `--directory --no-empty-directory` is what keeps a repo with `node_modules` from emitting 200k paths — plus, for every wildcard-free pattern, a targeted `['-C', repoRoot, 'check-ignore', '-q', '--', <pattern>]` so a file inside a wholly-collapsed ignored directory is still reachable. column8: Observable today. The key name, the value and the enabling mechanism are git's own and correct — the delta is a missing post-removal `git config --local --unset extensions.worktreeConfig`, plus the two pieces of state that gate it per the doc's carve-out: an "we added it" ownership marker taken BEFORE the first sparse-set, and a "no worktrees left" count taken AFTER the remove. Because the ownership probe has to happen before the entry exists, this cannot be retrofitted as a removal-only change. One Nessy-specific wrinkle: leases are per session under one shared per-repo namespace root (`<parent-of-repo>/.nessy-worktrees/<repo>/<leaseId>`, SessionManager.ts:10105-10110), so "last worktree" must be computed from git (`git worktree list --porcelain`), not from one `WorktreeLeaseService` instance's lease list.

Use `--local` explicitly on both read and write so a value in the user's global config is never read as ours and never unset. column7: Confined to the worktree lifecycle in packages/server-core, no wire or schema change if the marker-file design is used. Readers: `createPiWorktreeLeaseService` is the single construction site of `WorktreeLeaseService` (11 call sites in SessionManager.ts) and both its closures are called from `recoverUnlocked`, `releaseUnlocked` and `sweepOrphansUnlocked` (worktree-lease-service.ts:290-311, :317-337, :150-194), so the orphan sweep (SessionManager.ts:10064, :10758) inherits the cleanup for free. Tests touched: worktree-git-plan.test.ts only; the lease-service and orphan-sweep suites stay green because the port shape does not change. Sandbox: the unset runs through `runWorktreeGit` (SessionManager.ts:10020-10048) with `profile: 'read-only'` and `additionalWritableRoots: [root, namespaceRoot]`; `<root>/.git/config` sits inside `root` and is in no deny floor — `selfConfigDenyWriteRoots` denies only `.claude`/`.nessy-agent`/`.agents` and user-scope config (packages/server-core/src/pi-harness/isolation/self-config-deny.ts:59-73), and `sharedGitDirectoryGrant` (whose `deniedWriteRoots` DO include `config`) resolves to undefined here because the spawn's workspaceRoot is the containment root, not a linked worktree (isolation.ts:279-283). So no isolation change is needed — but if the project root is itself a linked worktree the shared `.git` lies outside every writable root, and the unset will be denied; `allowFailure` plus the swallow keeps that harmless. Explicit risk boundaries: (a) the change WRITES to the user's own repository `.git/config`, i.e. state Nessy does not own and cannot recreate — that is why the ownership probe, the count and the `config.worktree` guard are all preconditions, not niceties; (b) the marker file is new on-disk state under `<parent-of-repo>/.nessy-worktrees/<repo>/`, a filesystem persistence boundary shared across sessions and concurrent processes, so it must be created idempotently and removed only under the same gate; (c) if a future revision instead records ownership on `PiWorktreeLeaseV1` / `PiWorktreeLeaseStateV1` (packages/shared/src/sessions/types.ts:224-251) it crosses the persisted session-state boundary and becomes a schema risk trigger.

It surfaces the moment a user puts `worktree.sparsePaths` in `~/.nessy-agent/config.json` (read live per operation, SessionManager.ts:10116 via getUserWorktreeSettings, packages/shared/src/config/storage.ts:1313) and then uses a worktree — `EnterWorktree`, or a subagent worktree lease. Nothing in Nessy's UI mentions the entry or the fix, and the repository the user is left holding is their own.

column8: Concrete and shipped: every scheduled task edits the live checkout. A user who schedules "run the linter and fix findings nightly" or any refactor task gets a run that starts in the workspace default project directory with whatever uncommitted work is sitting there, mixes its edits into that dirty tree, and can conflict with an interactive session the user has open on the same files — the exact scenario the doc's Note tells them to avoid by enabling the toggle. There is no way to get the documented behaviour: the automation editor surfaces no such field (zero worktree hits across apps/electron/src/renderer/components/automations/), setting one by hand in automations.json is stripped at validation, and the two workarounds are both wrong-shaped — `worktree.bgIsolation: "worktree"` is global, applies to every session including interactive ones, and only blocks writes rather than creating a worktree (so a Claude- or Codex-backed scheduled run would just fail its first edit, since the release valve `EnterWorktree` is `visibility: 'pi-only'`), while instructing the prompt to call `EnterWorktree` works only for Pi-backed runs and only if the model complies. Latent second-order impact: two scheduled tasks firing on the same tick both mutate one working directory, so their edits interleave.

column5: The whole self-paced half of the page is absent, not mis-keyed. There is no `ScheduleWakeup` tool (no schema, no registry entry, no handler, no port method), no dynamic `/loop` iteration for it to re-arm or stop, no ~20-minute fallback wakeup, and no representation of a wakeup that is a delay rather than a cron expression — `SessionCronRecord` can only express a cron string, so even a correctly-named tool would have nothing to write. Two sub-deltas are narrower and independently real: (1) `cronJitterOffsetMs` would apply jitter to a dynamic loop, contradicting scheduled-tasks.md:74, because `SessionCronRecord` has no no-jitter field; (2) `session_crons` in Stop hook input is already correct by construction — anything stored as a record projects — so tools-reference.md:46's Stop-hook clause needs no work once the wakeup IS a record. The fixed-interval half of the page (5-field dialect, 8-char ids, 50 cap, seven-day expiry, ID-derived jitter, once-a-second tick, symlink refusal, `NESSY_DISABLE_CRON`/`CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_CRON`) is at parity and is not part of this divergence.

Relax `isRecord` (:153-165) so a record carrying them still validates and one lacking them still loads — both must stay optional or every existing on-disk store is discarded. Thread both through `create` (:224-245) and add a `rearm(id, nextFireAt)` method to the `SessionCronStore` interface (:187-204) that rewrites `nextFireAt` the way `markFired` (:255-259) rewrites `lastFiredAt`. column8: None observable today. A user cannot reach the missing mechanism at all: there is no `/loop` command to type (no bundled command or skill exists — `apps/electron/resources/skills/` holds only `plugin-creator` and `skill-creator`), so no self-paced iteration can start and no wakeup can be pending. What a user CAN do is ask in chat for a repeating check, which the model serves with `CronCreate` on a fixed cron schedule; the visible difference from Claude Code is that the interval never adapts — a poll set to 5m keeps polling every 5 minutes after the build goes quiet, and the model has no way to end its own loop other than `CronDelete`, which it must choose to call. It would surface the moment a `/loop` host ships: a self-paced loop would then either never re-arm (loop dies after one iteration) or, if built on `CronCreate` alone, run on a jittered fixed schedule that scheduled-tasks.md:74 says must not be jittered.

column5: The whole mechanism is missing — this is not a wrong key name or a wrong default. Three separate pieces are absent: (1) any per-session count of `web_search` calls; (2) the 200 default and its env lever (our spelling would be `NESSY_MAX_WEB_SEARCHES_PER_SESSION`, per this repo's documented rename convention at packages/shared/src/config/background-task-settings.ts:9-12); (3) the documented over-cap RESULT — a non-error notice telling the model to continue with what it has. Note the shape of (3): our failure path already returns `details: { isError: true }` (create-search-tool.ts:97, :109), and the cap must NOT use it, because the page explicitly contrasts the notice with "an error that would invite a retry". One further scope gap beyond the mechanism itself: because subagents are separate sessions/subprocesses, a counter that is merely per-process satisfies the default and the knob but not `tools-reference.md:432`'s "counted across the main conversation and every subagent it spawns" — a parallel research fan-out would get one full budget per child.

Two deliberate differences from retry.ts: no ceiling clamp (`env-vars.md:283` says "no upper bound"), and no per-call override, because the cap is not per call. Also export a tiny counter seam `createWebSearchBudget(limit: number, alreadyUsed = 0)` returning `{ limit, used(): number, tryConsume(): boolean }` so the enforcement point is unit-testable without a provider. Header comment must carry the mapping `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_WEB_SEARCHES_PER_SESSION` → `NESSY_MAX_WEB_SEARCHES_PER_SESSION` and cite `env-vars.md:283` + `tools-reference.md:432` verbatim, the way background-task-settings.ts:9-12 does. ~35 lines.; packages/pi-agent-server/src/tools/search/create-search-tool.ts (createSearchTool) — Add a third parameter `options?: { budget?: WebSearchBudget }` (keep it optional so the five existing test call sites and the two harness-contract fixtures keep compiling unchanged). At the top of `execute` (:68-70), BEFORE the provider call at :73, do `if (options?.budget && !options.budget.tryConsume()) return notice(...)`. `notice()` returns `{ content: [{ type: 'text', text: <notice> }], details: {} }` — deliberately WITHOUT `isError`, unlike the two failure returns at :90-99 and :102-110; `tools-reference.md:432` requires a notice "rather than an error that would invite a retry". Text must tell the model to continue with what it already gathered and name the lever, e.g. `Web search limit reached for this session (<limit> searches). Continue with the information you already gathered; if you genuinely need more searches, ask the user to raise NESSY_MAX_WEB_SEARCHES_PER_SESSION.` Consume exactly once per `execute` call, before the primary attempt, so the internal fallback attempt (:81) does not double-count and a provider failure still spends the call (the doc counts "WebSearch calls", not successes). ~12 lines.; packages/pi-agent-server/src/index.ts (webTools (:1393-1396) + a module-scope budget) — Create ONE budget for the process at module scope (not inside `buildSessionDefinition`, which is called a second time for the cwd-prepare candidate at :2951 — a per-closure counter would silently reset on a working-directory switch) and pass it: `createSearchTool(searchProvider, undefined, { budget: webSearchBudget })`. Seed it from `resolveMaxWebSearchesPerSession()`; the knob already reaches this process because PiAgent spawns it with `...process.env` (packages/shared/src/agent/pi-agent.ts:1462-1477). Do NOT put the cap on `InitMessage.orchestrator` (:232-244): that object is normalized into the signed manifest identity (`expectedOrchestrator: normalizePiOrchestratorConfig(...)` at :1531 and :1793), and the README's `maxParallelTasks` row (packages/pi-agent-server/README.md:47) records what adding a per-host number there costs — a manifest/model-contract mismatch that kills the first turn. ~6 lines.; packages/pi-agent-server/src/index.ts + packages/shared/src/agent/pi-harness/child-session-port.ts + packages/server-core/src/pi-harness/child-session-service.ts (InitMessage (:196-252) / PiChildStartInput+PiChildResult / ChildSessionService) — The cross-subagent half, and the only part that crosses a boundary. Because each subagent is its own session and subprocess (SessionManager.ts:10391 → createSession), the count must be host-owned per session TREE. Recommended shape: add one optional field `webSearchesUsed?: number` to `InitMessage` (a JSONL-only shape — do NOT touch `orchestrator`), seed the subprocess budget with it, and report consumption back to the host on the existing result/event channel; the host keeps the running total on the root session and passes the current value into every `PiChildStartInput` it starts, resolving the root through the existing `budgets.ancestry` (child-session-port.ts:6-15). Adding a numeric field to `PiChildBudgetsV1` is the alternative and is the more invasive one: that interface is part of the persisted `PiChildSessionRecordV1`/`PiChildSessionStateV1` (child-session-port.ts:60-101, `schemaVersion: 1`, written by `ChildSessionService.persist`), so it is a persistence-schema change. Either way a parallel fan-out can overshoot by up to the number of children started before their first report settles; record that as the accepted narrowing. If the plan chooses to ship enforcement per pi-subprocess ONLY, this entry is dropped, effort falls to M, and the narrowing ("one budget per session and per subagent, not one per tree") must be written into the audit row rather than left implicit.; packages/pi-agent-server/src/tools/search/create-search-tool.test.ts (new cases) — Two representative cases plus a table for the parser (the repo's minimum-non-duplicative rule): (1) with a budget of 1, the second `execute` returns the notice, `details.isError` is undefined, and the provider's `search` was called exactly once — the negative path AND the proof the provider is not reached; (2) a provider failure still consumes one unit (so a failing search cannot loop for free). column8: None observable in ordinary use — no wrong output, no missing UI. It surfaces the moment a turn loops on search, which is exactly the case the cap exists for, and there is no backstop at all: the model can issue unlimited `web_search` calls in one session, and a `subagent` fan-out multiplies that with no shared ceiling. Two concrete consequences. On the default Nessy Gateway/Pi connection the provider is DuckDuckGo, so a loop hammers three DDG endpoints with up to three retries each (packages/pi-agent-server/src/tools/search/providers/ddg.ts:38-59, :202-227); DDG answers with its anomaly/"too quickly" throttle, so the user watches searches get slower and then start failing, with each failure feeding a `Search failed…` block into context instead of a notice telling the model to stop and use what it has. On an OpenAI-API-key, ChatGPT-subscription or Google-key connection every single call is a billed upstream request (packages/pi-agent-server/src/tools/search/resolve-provider.ts:58-86, providers/chatgpt.ts:100-110), so the same loop spends real quota or money with nothing to stop it. What would make it visible deliberately: a research prompt that keeps searching, or a `subagent` fan-out of research agents — today each child gets its own unlimited budget.

column5: This is not a wrong key name or a wrong value — the whole Markdown-awareness pass is missing. Precisely: (a) fenced code blocks are NOT skipped; a line inside ``` or ~~~ whose trimmed start is `@<path>` is followed, and the fence is corrupted — the body is spliced in on the inlining route (memory-store.ts:104-106) and the line is deleted on the pinned route (base-agent.ts:1005). (b) Code spans ARE skipped, but only as a by-product of the line-start-only gate, and that same by-product simultaneously violates memory.md:101's "anywhere in your CLAUDE.md" — no mid-line import is ever followed. So the code-span rule is currently satisfied by breaking a neighbouring rule, and any later fix that makes mid-line imports work will silently re-open the code-span hole unless a real scanner lands first. The correct unit of repair is one shared markdown-aware line scanner consumed by all three call sites, not a per-line tweak in `parseMemoryImportPath`.

column8: Concrete and reachable today. Any MEMORY.md, `.agents/rules/*.md` or `.claude/rules/*.md` that DOCUMENTS an import inside a fenced code block — which is exactly what Claude's own memory.md does, and what any repo's "how to write memory files" section does — has that example silently executed. Measured output for a user MEMORY.md whose ```text fence contains `@secret.md`: the `<memory>` block the model receives reads "```text / SECRET_IMPORTED_BODY / ```". So the user sees (a) an instruction file that no longer says what they wrote, with a corrupted code fence, (b) an unintended file loaded into every turn's context, spending budget, and (c) in Sources, the fenced target listed as an imported memory capability they never asked for, carrying its own enable/disable toggle. On the pinned-capability route the failure is the mirror image: the fenced `@path` line is deleted, so a documentation example loses its middle line with no explanation. Worst realistic case is exfiltration-shaped: a CLAUDE.md that merely mentions `@~/.ssh/config` inside a fence pulls the file into context. The code-span half is NOT observable today — the line-start-only gate hides it — and would surface only if mid-line imports (memory.md:101, "anywhere in your CLAUDE.md") were implemented without a real scanner.

column8: A user who follows Claude's documented practice and puts `<!-- maintainer note -->` in AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, CLAUDE.local.md or MEMORY.md gets the opposite of what the doc promises: the note is sent to the model inside the pinned `<capability-layer>` block on every capability generation, it spends context tokens the doc says it will not, and the model can act on a line addressed to human maintainers (a stale 'TODO: drop this rule' comment reads as an instruction). This repo's own AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md contain no HTML comments (grep -a), so it is latent here; it surfaces the moment a user or an imported Claude plugin ships an instruction file that uses them, and it surfaces immediately for anyone who moved a CLAUDE.md over from Claude Code, where the comments were free.

column5: The whole mechanism is absent: no writer inspects the first line for `---`, and no key named `modified` is ever emitted, so a memory file that DOES begin with frontmatter is appended to and left with a stale (or missing) timestamp forever. This is not a wrong key name for a right value: Nessy's nearest artefact, `<!-- nessy:auto:YYYY-MM-DD -->`, differs on all four axes the doc fixes -- location (trailing HTML comment on the bullet, not a frontmatter key), granularity (one date per entry, not one timestamp per file), precision (calendar day, not ISO-8601 instant) and audience (stripped at load, so the model never sees it, versus a value the doc puts in front of both user and model). Renaming it would satisfy nothing. Conversely the doc's negative half is already satisfied by accident, not by design: because both writers seed a new file as `# Memory\n\n- ...`, Nessy never adds frontmatter to a file that has none -- so the observable gap is confined to files whose frontmatter a human hand-authored. One second-order divergence rides along and constrains the fix: Claude Code strips frontmatter before loading the index (`memory.md:388`, min-version 2.1.211), while `readMemoryFile` (`memory-store.ts:29-33`) reads the raw first 200 lines, so in this fork a frontmatter block -- and any `modified:` line we add -- becomes prompt content inside the `<memory>` block rather than metadata.

column8: None observable for any file the app itself created: both writers seed a new MEMORY.md as `# Memory` plus bullets, so no Nessy-generated memory file has frontmatter for the field to live in. It surfaces the moment a user hand-authors a frontmatter header on their memory file -- e.g. a `---\ntitle: ...\n---` block at the top of `~/.nessy-agent/MEMORY.md` or a project MEMORY.md, which is a normal thing to do to a markdown file they were told they may edit freely (memory.md: 'plain markdown you can edit or delete at any time'). From then on every save -- the agent's `remember` tool and the chat UI's remember action alike -- appends a bullet and leaves that header frozen, so neither the user opening the file nor the model reading it back can tell whether a fact is from today or from three months ago. Today the model gets no freshness signal at all: the only date Nessy records, the per-entry `<!-- nessy:auto:DATE -->` marker, is stripped in mergeMemoryContents before the prompt is built (memory-store.ts:173), so it exists solely so the cleanup sweep can tell agent lines from human ones. What would make the gap visible in a test rather than in the wild: any fixture MEMORY.md that starts with `---`.

column5: The entire synchronous post-write feedback loop is absent — this is not a key-name or value mismatch, there is nothing to rename. Three distinct pieces are missing: (1) no measurement of `MEMORY.md` after a write, so neither the near-limit reminder nor the over-limit error is ever produced on either writer; (2) the 25KB byte limit does not exist as a concept anywhere in the fork — only the 200-line one, and only as a load-time slice, never as a write-time check; (3) the documented measurement exclusion (YAML frontmatter and block-level HTML comments stripped before measuring) has no counterpart, because nothing measures. One rationale caveat matters for the fix: the doc's justification "everything past the limit is dropped on the next load" holds only on our legacy fallback composer (system.ts:453-455 → readMemoryFile's 200-line slice). On the shipped capability path nothing is dropped at all — the whole file is pinned every turn (base-agent.ts:976-1015 → materializer.ts:169-186), so the harm there is unbounded pinned-context growth rather than silent truncation. Both harms are real; a fix must decide which limit it is enforcing on which path.

column8: Two different harms, by path, and neither is signalled anywhere. On the shipped capability path (capabilityContextPinned true) nothing is dropped: MEMORY.md grows without bound and its whole content is pinned into every turn, so a long-lived workspace's memory silently consumes context and tokens, and the user's only clue is the /context overlay's generic `trim_memory_files` hint, which fires on token share rather than on the limit. On the legacy fallback path (prompts/system.ts:453-455) everything past line 200 is silently dropped at load, so a user who can see a fact in MEMORY.md gets an agent that has never read it — no error, no transcript note, no Memory-UI marker. Reaching either state today takes roughly 200 `remember` calls or a hand-edited long MEMORY.md, so for most users it is latent; it surfaces first on shared project MEMORY.md files that people also edit by hand.

column5: The whole write-time mechanism is absent — not misnamed, not narrower. Nothing measures the index after a write, so neither documented output exists: not the hard over-limit error, and not the milder near-limit reminder. Both writers return a bare unconditional success (`Saved memory to <path>` for the model; `{success:true,scope}` for the UI). Secondary deltas that make the doc's error text untrue until they are fixed too: the 25KB byte limit does not exist at all; the 200-line limit exists only as a silent slice on the LEGACY composer and is entirely absent on the live capability path, so on the default path nothing is dropped (the whole oversized index is pinned every turn instead); and the measurement's documented exclusion of YAML frontmatter and block-level HTML comments has no implementation. The pre-v2.1.210 behaviour the page names as the defect ("an over-limit index was silently truncated on the next load with no write-time signal") is exactly what the legacy path does today.

column8: Today nothing ever tells a user their memory index has outgrown its read limit. On the legacy (non-pinned-capability) composer every line past 200 stops reaching the model — the user keeps saying "remember this", the tool answers `Saved memory to …/MEMORY.md` every single time, and the oldest entries are already invisible with no signal anywhere. On the live capability-runtime path the failure inverts: no cap is applied at all, so an oversized index is pinned into EVERY turn and silently eats context budget instead. The observable surface is identical in both cases — an unconditional success in the tool result, an unconditional "memory saved" toast on the Save-to-memory UI path (ChatDisplay.tsx:1567), and never a prompt to compact the index. It surfaces the moment an index passes ~200 lines or ~25KB; a small index (this repo's own is well under) shows nothing, which is why the gap is easy to miss.

column8: Latent for an individual user; immediate and silent for the first org that follows the page. A platform/IT team that deploys `CLAUDE.md` to the system directory — the same directory from which this fork already reads `managed-policy.json`, so the deployment channel is believed to work — gets no effect and no error: the org standards never enter the pinned capability block, no loaded-memory list mentions the file, and nothing reports that it was ignored. column8: In a Claude-backend session, an automation that blocks a prompt on `UserPromptSubmit` refuses the prompt and tells the user nothing about why. The hook's reason string reaches the SDK (hooks-automation.ts:1673-1683), comes back only on the `informational` banner, and the adapter discards it. What the user sees is the turn ending with no explanation — not literal silence, because the SDK still emits a `result` and adaptResult (:581-601) turns that into a bare completion or a generic 'Query failed'. The identical automation under Pi, Codex or Nestor Cloud prints the reason as an error message, so this is a visible per-backend inconsistency for anyone with prompt-gating automations. The same missing branch also swallows every other loop banner Claude sends — non-error status lines and `warning`/`suggestion`-level notices — so an enabled-Claude user is quietly missing a whole display channel the other three backends have. Latent in the shipped default build (NESSY_FEATURE_PROVIDER_CLAUDE off); it surfaces the moment a Claude-enabled build meets any configured UserPromptSubmit automation.

column5: The entire cap is absent — not a wrong constant, not a wrong key name, and not enforcement one layer up. All three of the page's obligations are missing together: no byte accounting (so no cap), therefore no clear error and no non-zero exit on breach. Two shape details the fix must get right, because getting either wrong would satisfy the letter and miss the point. (1) The cap must be measured on RAW BYTES read from the pipe (`value.byteLength`), not on the decoded string's `.length` — a UTF-8 multibyte payload would otherwise pass a character-count check well past 10MB. (2) It must fail FAST, cancelling the reader the moment the running total crosses the ceiling, not after the loop drains: the current code holds every chunk in `chunks` and then joins, so peak memory is roughly twice the input, and a post-hoc length check would still let a multi-gigabyte pipe exhaust memory before the error could be printed — which is the failure the cap exists to prevent. Separately, the error must reach the user as a clear message on BOTH paths: a throw from `cmdSend` is already caught by main()'s handler (apps/cli/src/index.ts:2242-2245 → `err(msg)` + `process.exit(1)`), but `run` is dispatched at :2132, BEFORE that `try` opens at :2184, so a throw out of `cmdRun` escapes main() entirely as an unhandled rejection instead of the documented clear error.
column6: apps/cli/src/index.ts (MAX_PIPED_STDIN_BYTES (new) + readPrompt (:423-442)) — Add `export const MAX_PIPED_STDIN_BYTES = 10 * 1024 * 1024` immediately above `readPrompt`, with a comment citing headless.md:88. Inside the stdin branch, keep a `let bytes = 0`; after each successful `read()`, do `bytes += value.byteLength` and, when `bytes > MAX_PIPED_STDIN_BYTES`, `await reader.cancel()` and `throw new Error('Piped input exceeds the 10MB stdin limit. Write the content to a file and reference the file path in your prompt instead of piping it.')` BEFORE pushing the chunk — the cancel-then-throw ordering is what keeps peak memory bounded. Also append `chunks.push(decoder.decode())` after the loop to flush the streaming decoder (today a trailing incomplete multibyte sequence is silently dropped). Change the signature to `export async function readPrompt(words: string[], restArgs?: string[], stdinStream: ReadableStream<Uint8Array> = Bun.stdin.stream())` and read from `stdinStream.getReader()` at :430 — that default-parameter injection is the only test seam available, since the function is currently module-private and codegraph reports no covering tests. Do NOT call `process.exit` inside `readPrompt`; throwing keeps it unit-testable and matches how the schema gate already reports (:583-588).; apps/cli/src/index.ts (cmdRun (:764-770)) — Wrap the `await readPrompt(args.rest, args.rest)` call at :766 in a `try { ... } catch (e) { err(e instanceof Error ? e.message : String(e)); process.exit(1) }`, byte-for-byte the shape of the schema gate four lines below it (:774-780). Required, not cosmetic: `run` is dispatched at :2132, outside main()'s `try` (:2184), so without this the throw leaves main() as an unhandled rejection and the user gets a stack trace rather than the documented clear error. `cmdSend` (:576) needs no change — main()'s catch at :2242-2245 already turns the throw into `Error: <msg>` on stderr plus `process.exit(1)`.; apps/cli/src/commands.test.ts (new `describe('readPrompt stdin cap')` beside the existing `parseArgs` block) — Two cases, using the injected stream (`new ReadableStream({ start(c) { c.enqueue(new Uint8Array(n)); c.close() } })`) and importing `readPrompt, MAX_PIPED_STDIN_BYTES` from './index.ts' alongside the existing `parseArgs` import: (1) positive — a payload of exactly `MAX_PIPED_STDIN_BYTES` bytes resolves and the returned string has the expected length, proving the boundary is inclusive; (2) negative — `MAX_PIPED_STDIN_BYTES + 1` bytes delivered as two chunks rejects with a message containing '10MB', asserted via `expect(readPrompt([], ['--stdin'], stream)).rejects.toThrow(/10MB/)`. A third cheap case is worth it: enqueue a chunk far over the cap and assert the stream's `cancel` was observed (a `cancel()` spy on the ReadableStream source), which is what proves fail-fast rather than drain-then-check.; docs/cli.md (the stdin examples at :121-125 (send) and :196-199 (run)) — One sentence after each block stating that piped stdin is capped at 10MB and that a larger input exits non-zero with an error, pointing at the write-to-a-file workaround. The fork's own CLI reference currently documents the piping surface with no limit, so it would otherwise contradict the new behaviour.

column8: Observable, but only with a large pipe. `cat big.log | nessy-general-agent run "what is failing?"` — the exact form docs/cli.md:196-199 recommends — is accepted at any size with no warning. At tens of MB the run appears to succeed while the whole file is joined into one prompt string, so the user's real experience is a silently exhausted context window and a truncated or confused answer, with no message telling them the input was too big. Push it further and the failure mode becomes wrong rather than merely quiet: peak CLI memory is roughly twice the input (every chunk retained in `chunks` before `join`), so a multi-hundred-MB pipe ends in a Bun allocation failure or an OOM kill; and once the serialized text frame passes the `ws` 100 MiB default the connection is closed mid-send, which surfaces to the user as `Error: Send timeout — no completion event received` from sendAndStream (:562) — a transport timeout, not "piped stdin is capped at 10MB". So today the user gets, in order of input size: silent context exhaustion, then a misleading timeout, then a crash — never the documented clear error. The same holds for `send` with `--stdin` (docs/cli.md:124).

column8: None observable today. A user who picks Concise, Explanatory, Reviewer or a custom style on Settings → AI does get the style on every request, because `getSystemPrompt` re-runs per turn (pi-agent.ts:6586, claude-agent.ts:1244) and the block is re-sent inside the system prompt each time. So there is no surface where the style is simply missing. What is absent is the reinforcement Claude Code relies on, and it would surface as instruction drift rather than as an error: a strict-format custom style (a required answer template, a mandated marker) that holds early and is quietly dropped deep in a long session, where the model has since accumulated many competing per-turn instruction blocks on the user tail — and after a compaction, which rewrites the history between the system prefix and the current turn. Nothing in the UI tells the user the style is still active, so the drift reads as the app ignoring the setting. Making it surface requires a long, tool-heavy session with a hard-formatting custom style; a short conversation will not show it.

(1) The new first stdout line changes the stream-json contract: every consumer of `nessy-general-agent run|send --output-format stream-json` must tolerate a leading non-`session:event` object. Existing consumers in-repo are the tests at apps/cli/src/run.test.ts:213, :338, :372 and the docs at docs/cli.md:165. (2) If the frame is instead added as a new `SessionEvent`/`AgentEvent` member (the alternative to CLI-side synthesis), it touches packages/core/src/types/message.ts:966-1014 and packages/shared/src/protocol/dto.ts:342-... — both are read by the Electron renderer's event reducers as well as the CLI, so every exhaustive switch over the union becomes a compile site. column8: Concrete and current, though it only bites on the headless surface. A CI job running `nessy-general-agent run --output-format stream-json ... | jq` gets a stream whose first line is already a `text_delta`/`tool_start`; if an enabled MCP source was skipped because its config failed validation (stdio entry with no `command`, HTTP entry with no `url`, or an authenticated source with no token), the run proceeds with that server's tools simply absent and the job sees NO signal — the reason exists only in a `debug()` string that is off unless debug logging is enabled (packages/shared/src/sources/server-builder.ts:110, :127, :164), and the aggregated error list is dropped before anyone can read it (packages/shared/src/mcp/runtime-pool-servers.ts:392 → :428). The observed failure is therefore a silent quality regression: the agent answers without the tool it was supposed to have, and the pipeline exits 0. A terminal (`--output-format text`) run is equally silent — the startup output stops at 'LLM connection configured:' (apps/cli/src/index.ts:759). Second, smaller impact: a consumer written against Claude's stream-json contract crashes or drops the run when its first-line init parse finds no `system`/`init` object.

column5: The `system/init` frame does not exist, so all four CI-gating arrays (`plugins`, `plugin_errors`, `mcp_servers`, `mcp_server_errors`) and the optional `capabilities` array are absent from the headless stream, as is `system/api_retry`. This is a missing frame, not a key-name mismatch: there is no member of any spelling on `AgentEvent`/`SessionEvent` carrying plugin or MCP load state. Two sub-deltas differ in nature and must not be treated alike. (1) `plugin_errors` is a PROJECTION gap — the demotion set is already computed and already omitted-when-empty (`ResolvedInstalledPlugin.dependencyErrors`, resolver.ts:697-703, plus the three demoting diagnostics at resolver.ts:1870-1908); only the key names differ (`code` vs `type`, plugin `name` vs `plugin`) and no frame carries it. Likewise `plugins[].path`: the value exists as `bundleRootPath` (resolver.ts:709) and is deliberately stripped from the Safe view, so it needs a new non-Safe projection, not a Safe-view change. (2) `mcp_server_errors` is a MISSING PRODUCER — nothing anywhere records an MCP server skipped for invalid config; native-sources.ts:562-566 swallows the parse failure. `mcp_servers[].status` is half-present: `McpPoolHealth.connected/failed` gives per-slug status but only after the Pi runtime has started, which is after the first turn, i.e. after the point the doc puts the init frame. `capabilities` is the weakest binding of the set — the page says the field "requires Claude Code v2.1.205 or later and is absent from earlier versions", so a consumer must tolerate its absence; we also have no protocol-capability names to put in it (`grep -ran 'interrupt_receipt' packages apps` → 0 hits). Two items in the original claim's enumeration are NOT divergences and stay out of the fix: the stream does terminate (`complete`, dto.ts:351, handled at apps/cli/src/index.ts:516-535) and that frame does carry cost (`TokenUsage.costUsd`, packages/core/src/types/message.ts:500-505) — only the spelling `total_cost_usd` differs.

column7: Crosses a wire boundary twice, which is a risk trigger in this repo. (1) The new RPC channel touches packages/shared/src/protocol/channels.ts and the routing allowlist in packages/shared/src/protocol/routing.ts; any channel not in that allowlist is unreachable, and the electron transport map (apps/electron/src/transport/channel-map.ts:224 pattern) is where a renderer consumer would have to be added if one is ever wanted. (2) The `api_retry` half adds a member to `AgentEvent` (packages/core/src/types/message.ts:966) and `SessionEvent` (packages/shared/src/protocol/dto.ts:343) — both are consumed by the electron renderer's `session:event` handling and by the CLI passthrough, and every exhaustive switch over the union must tolerate it. Note the validator trap on the neighbouring path: packages/shared/src/protocol/pi-harness-runtime.ts:100 asserts an EXACT key set on the harness snapshot (`exact(input, [… 'mcpHealth' …])`), so if a fixer chooses to extend the harness snapshot instead of adding the new channel, that allowlist and the `mcpHealth` validator at :177 must be updated or validation throws. The capability-resolver edits are read by everything that consumes `EffectiveCapabilitySnapshot`: toUserCatalog / toSafeInstalledPlugin (packages/shared/src/capabilities/views.ts:382-498, the renderer catalog), the materializer (packages/shared/src/capabilities/materializer.ts:86, :241), runtime-output-styles.ts:24, and the capabilities RPC surface (packages/server-core/src/handlers/rpc/capabilities.ts, with its test suite at packages/server-core/src/handlers/rpc/__tests__/capabilities.test.ts). The path-free invariant on `SafeInstalledPluginSummary` (packages/shared/src/protocol/capabilities.ts:289-320, 'Names/status only; no paths, commands, URLs or secret refs' at :880) is the boundary that must NOT be relaxed to obtain `plugins[].path` — a Safe-view change would leak bundle paths to the renderer. Imported-plugin paths matter here: the demoted-plugin set the frame reports comes from `plugin-dependencies` resolution over Claude- and Codex-format bundles, so both format adapters feed it. No persistence boundary is crossed: the init frame is derived, nothing new is written to disk.
column8: Concrete and silent. Today `nessy-general-agent run --output-format stream-json` in CI emits only our own turn events — the first line is a `text_delta`/`tool_start`, never metadata — so a pipeline cannot tell which model, which plugins or which MCP servers the run actually had. When an installed plugin is demoted (unsatisfied declared dependency, missing required MCP env var, unset `user_config` key — the states resolver.ts:697-703 and :1870-1908 already compute) or an MCP source fails to connect or has a malformed `config.json`, the run proceeds with those tools and skills simply absent, prints a plausible answer, and exits 0. The CI job goes green on a degraded agent: a Bash-guard `PreToolUse` hook that never loaded is the worst case, because the gate the pipeline believes it has is not running. The desktop control center CAN see degraded MCP state (`mcpHealth {status, connected, failed}`, SessionManager.ts:3178) — the headless surface cannot, so the same failure is visible in the GUI and invisible in CI. Partial workaround a user has today: run `nessy-general-agent doctor --json` as a separate step, which exits 1 on `unfulfilledPluginMandates` (apps/cli/src/doctor.ts:219-222) — it covers mandated-but-not-installed only, not an installed plugin that failed to load, and nothing about MCP servers.

column5: The whole mechanism is absent — this is not a key-name or value mismatch that a rename would fix. Four separable pieces are missing: (1) `policyHelper` is not a recognised managed key, so the admin-authored value is stripped rather than read; (2) nothing spawns the executable at `path` with `timeoutMs`, so no `managedSettings` envelope is ever parsed; (3) the managed tier has no helper seam, so even a parsed helper output could not become the single winning source ahead of `delivered` and `file`; (4) there is no `refreshIntervalMs` re-run timer and no non-zero-exit startup refusal for it. The precedence RULE we do implement is correct for the two sources we have — winner-takes-all, no merge (`packages/shared/src/config/managed-composition.ts:184-214`) — so the delta is the missing top rung of that ordering, not a wrong ordering. Scope note on the recorded justification: `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-07-28-server-managed-delivery.md:212-215` puts `policyHelper` out of scope as "OS-policy sources only", which correctly excludes it from the server-DELIVERED channel (settings.md:633 agrees it is ignored there) but says nothing about the system-FILE scope, which the same sentence names as valid and which this fork ships. The audit row is `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-29-deviation-audit.md:193` (R25b, "Record as C" = documented, not implemented) — an open item, not a closed owner decision.

Add a `parsePolicyHelper` branch in `parsePolicy` under the tolerant sink: `path` a required absolute string (reject relative, reject `~`), `timeoutMs` an optional positive finite number with a bounded default, `refreshIntervalMs` an optional number that is either exactly `0` or `>= 60000` per the doc's table — any defect drops the WHOLE `policyHelper` object as `stripped` (never a partial helper config), matching the tolerant posture the file's docblock at :1487-1497 states. column8: None observable for ordinary users — latent, and administrator-facing. Concretely today: an admin who follows Claude's page and deploys `{"policyHelper": {"path": "/usr/local/bin/nessy-policy", "refreshIntervalMs": 300000}}` in the system managed-policy file gets the key silently ignored as policy and loudly ignored as a diagnostic — `refuseUnknownKeys` records `invalid managed Pi policy key: policyHelper` (managed-policy.ts:731), `reportManagedPolicyDrops` prints `[managed-settings] …` to stderr/the main log at startup (managed-drops.ts:190 via storage-runtime.ts:247), and the same drop appears under `Invalid managed entries` in `nessy-general-agent doctor` (config-doctor.ts:446-451). The app then starts and enforces whatever the static file or the delivered payload says. Nothing crashes and nothing is mis-enforced, so an end user sees nothing at all; what the organisation loses is the ability to derive policy from device posture, identity or a remote service, and the ability to have a per-device policy refresh on an interval it chooses. It surfaces the moment an admin deploys the key and either reads the startup log or runs the doctor.

column8: A user cannot rebind any keyboard shortcut in Nessy Desktop, and there is no surface that tells them so. Settings -> Shortcuts (ShortcutsPage.tsx) and the Cmd+/ Keyboard Shortcuts dialog both render the 27 defaults as static `<kbd>` chips with no edit affordance and no link to a config file; typing `/keybindings` in the composer matches no command. Concretely: `mod+q` is hardwired to app.quit, `escape` to chat.stopProcessing, `mod+a` to navigator.selectAll — a user whose muscle memory or accessibility setup needs a different chord has no route, and a user arriving from Claude Code who drops a `~/.claude/keybindings.json`-shaped file anywhere sees it silently ignored (no warning, no debug line). column5: The whole mechanism is absent, in four separable pieces. (1) No reader for the `subagentStatusLine` key at any scope — user, project, or managed — so the documented settings object is inert wherever a user writes it. (2) No per-refresh-tick command runner for it and no NDJSON `{"id","content"}` parser, hence no row-override, no hide-on-empty-content, no keep-default-on-omitted-id. (3) The plugin-shipped default is swallowed: a Claude bundle whose `settings.json` declares it is recorded as `plugin.deferred.claude_settings` with no author-facing warning (claude.ts:2275 has no `refusal`) — the same silent-deferral shape as f053, which owns that half. A user who copies a Claude `settings.json` containing `subagentStatusLine` into the fork gets no change and no error: the agent panel below the prompt keeps rendering its built-in `agent · task · status` row (AgentPanel.tsx:233-260), which is itself narrower than Claude's documented default because it shows no token count. column5: The whole missed-run mechanism is absent, not narrowed: no persisted per-task last-occurrence cursor, no start-time sweep, no wake trigger, no seven-day window, no discard-older rule, no catch-up notification. Two specifics that shape the fix. (a) It is not enough to make the sweep re-emit `SchedulerTick`: `matchesBasePredicate` (utils.ts:289) evaluates the cron against the CURRENT minute, so a replayed tick matches nothing — the sweep needs its own matcher-selection path, not a synthetic tick. (b) The nearest existing timestamp, automation history `ts` (webhook-utils.ts:65), is the RUN time, not the scheduled occurrence, and is capped at 20 entries per matcher; using it as the cursor would double-fire or silently skip. The cursor must be the OCCURRENCE time and must live in its own durable file. The sibling session-scoped Cron tier already has the correct discipline and the correct reason written down (packages/server-core/src/sessions/session-cron-service.ts:144-165: stamp at delivery, not enqueue; packages/shared/src/sessions/cron-scheduler.ts:121-131), but it implements the opposite contract (scheduled-tasks.md:215 forbids per-interval catch-up), is per-session and non-durable, and explicitly is not `SchedulerService` (session-cron-service.ts:9-16) — so it supplies a pattern to copy, not the behaviour.

Lives at `join(workspaceRootPath, AUTOMATIONS_SCHEDULE_STATE_FILE)`; `workspaceRootPath` is the managed workspace dir (packages/shared/src/workspaces/paths.ts:50), the same directory as automations.json and automations-history.jsonl. column8: Concrete and silent. A user creates a scheduled automation in the Automations UI — say cron `0 9 * * *` with a prompt action — and closes the laptop overnight. At 9am nothing happens. When they open the app at 11am, no session appears under the automation, no notification is shown, the card still reads "last ran" from whenever the machine last happened to be awake at 9am, and the run history has no entry at all — not even a skipped one — so there is nothing to tell them the run was lost. Claude Desktop would start exactly one catch-up session on wake and notify. Every scheduled automation whose cron time falls outside app uptime is affected, which for a daily-morning automation on a laptop is most days; the shorter the interval, the less it matters (an every-15-minutes task loses one occurrence and the next one arrives soon).

column8: A user installs a Claude Code plugin whose StopFailure hook alerts on API failures — the documented recipe reads `input=$(cat)` then `jq -r .error` / `.error_details` / `.last_assistant_message`. On a rate-limited or auth-failed turn the hook does fire, and matcher filtering picks the right hook, but all three reads return null: the Slack/log line the user gets is empty where the error type and text should be, so they learn a turn failed and nothing about why. Only Nessy's own Pi/native backend is affected; with NESSY_FEATURE_PROVIDER_CLAUDE on, the Claude SDK supplies the fields itself.

column8: Concrete and silent. A user pastes the JSON block from an MCP vendor's own quickstart — most publish `"type": "streamable-http"`, which is the MCP spec's name for the transport — into the project `.mcp.json` (or `~/.nessy-agent/mcp.json`, or `<project>/.nessy-agent/mcp.json`). The capability inventory still records the entry (native-sources.ts:493-509 creates one record per declared key regardless of `type`, and resolver.ts:1642-1655 turns that into a catalogue/MCP-panel summary whose transport falls back to `http`), so the server LOOKS configured, but the pool never receives it (runtime-pool-servers.ts:461-466 drops the parsed `undefined`) and none of its tools ever appear. The only diagnosis is the debug-channel line `Ignoring .mcp.json server "<name>": unsupported MCP server config` — nothing in the UI says the word `streamable-http`. On top of that, the pre-trust "this project provides N MCP servers" consent list undercounts, because it is built from the same parser (project-contribution-detect.ts:129), so the user approves a project without seeing the server that is being declared. Editing `streamable-http` to `http` by hand fixes it, which is exactly the manual step the doc sentence says should not be needed.

Two second-order deltas ride along. (a) Name collision: our module constant is spelled `MCP_CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MS`, which is a REAL but DIFFERENT Claude env var (env-vars.md:406, default 5000, the blocking-startup batch wait) — exposing our constant under its current name would ship a var whose name means something else upstream. (b) Budget shape: Claude's `MCP_TIMEOUT` "bounds an individual server's connect attempt", whereas our 3-attempt initial-connect retry (`MCP_CONNECT_RETRY = { attempts: 3, baseDelayMs: 250 }`, workspace-mcp-pool-registry.ts:784) runs INSIDE the one 30 s deadline (mcp-pool.ts:1202 races `connectWithRetries` against the deadline), so all attempts share the budget.

column8: Observable, and it hits the exact scenario the page's troubleshooting accordion is written for. A user adds a stdio MCP source whose first launch cold-downloads its package (`npx -y @playwright/mcp@latest` and similar) and needs more than 30 s: the connect is abandoned at the deadline (mcp-pool.ts:1196), the reconcile records the slug as failed (mcp-pool.ts:1509-1513) and reports it through `failedSlugsForLeaser` (:1651), so the source shows as failed in Sources and its tools are absent from that turn. The user then does what the Claude troubleshooting page tells them to do — set `MCP_TIMEOUT=60000` — and nothing changes, with no message explaining why, because no code reads it. There is no per-server escape either: a `timeout` field in `.mcp.json` is routed to tool-execution time (project-config.ts:98), not startup. In practice the source recovers on a later sync once the package cache is warm (mcp-pool.ts:1505 retries connects for slugs without a live client), so the damage is repeated startup failures and an unusable documented remedy rather than a permanent outage. Users on fast networks with warm caches never see it.

column5: Two deltas, both in delivery semantics of a feature we do ship — not absence. (a) IDLE ARRIVAL IS NOT SUPPORTED. The doc's only precondition is that the session is open; ours is that a turn is in flight. And the cause is one layer deeper than the `canDeliver()` gate the finding cites: the subscription is created and destroyed with the turn, so an event arriving between turns has no listener to reach and is discarded inside `McpClientPool.dispatchChannelMessage` before any session-level gate runs. Fixing only `canDeliver` would change nothing. (b) NO GROUPING. Several events during a busy turn are each `redirect()`-ed into the running turn immediately, where the contract is one grouped delivery in arrival order on the NEXT turn. Note what is NOT wrong: the policy/gate layer (`ChannelPolicy`, `resolveManagedChannelPolicy`, fail-closed default) is correct and deliberate, and the grouped-delivery machinery already exists — this is a wiring gap between `pool.subscribeChannel` and `deliverMonitorEvent`, plus a lifetime change on the subscription. Adjacent and NOT part of this delta (it gates any live verification): our client reads `params.text` (`packages/shared/src/mcp/client.ts:357-361`) while the documented field is `params.content`, and we never emit the `<channel source=... >` wrapper or `meta` attributes.

column7: One production subscriber (`SessionManager.ts:2436`), so the code fan-out is small — but the delivery mechanism changes class, and that is the risk. column8: None observable on a stock install: the switch is off by default, so no dispatcher is installed and no server can push at all. Two steps surface it. (1) Settings → Permissions → "Allow MCP servers to interject" (`PermissionsSettingsPage.tsx:256-262`). (2) Connect an MCP server that sends `notifications/claude/channel` with `params.text`. Then the page's headline scenario fails exactly as advertised-not-to: the user walks away, CI or a chat bridge posts an event, and nothing happens — no turn starts, no notification appears, and the pushing server gets no error back, because the event is discarded inside the pool with no listener present. It appears to work only if the user happens to be mid-turn, and then it is injected as a raw steer into whatever the agent was already doing, one steer per event, rather than as a grouped, framed background notification on the next turn. For a spec-conformant channel plugin the fix alone is still not user-visible, because our client reads `params.text` while the documented field is `params.content` — that key mismatch has to be closed too before a live channel smoke can pass.

column8: A user who writes the documented thing gets a broken server with a near-useless error. Put `"command": "${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}/scripts/mcp-server.js"` (or `"args": ["${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}/..."]`, or an `env` entry) in a repo's `.mcp.json`, open that project, and the entry is spawned with the literal string `${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}/scripts/mcp-server.js` as the executable — it fails ENOENT and the server shows as failed/disconnected in the MCP/Sources list. The only diagnostic is a debug-channel line, "references unset environment variables with no default", which names the variable but not that the host was supposed to supply it. Separately, any project-scoped stdio server that reads `CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR` from its own environment (the normal pattern for a repo-local server that must not hardcode a path) sees it undefined and either silently falls back to `cwd` or refuses to start. For imported Claude plugins the same reference fails too, through the wrong-key path — the process does carry `CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR`, but the manifest's token was rewritten to a name nothing sets, so `${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}` in a plugin's MCP command is broken while reading `$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR` inside the server works. That split is the most confusing surface here.

column5: Not a wrong key name and not a missing value: the positional family is simply not implemented on the command path. `$ARGUMENTS` and the legacy Nessy `{{args}}` expand correctly; `$0`, `$1`, `$ARGUMENTS[N]` and `\$1` escaping do not, so those placeholders reach the model as literal text. The correct 0-based, quote-aware, single-pass implementation the page describes already exists 200 lines away in `runtime-skill-content.ts` but is module-private and reachable only from the skill materializer. Second-order: the plugin importer's detector for the same construct is `/\$[1-9]\b/`, which misses `$0` (the FIRST argument per skills.md:302) and `$ARGUMENTS[N]` entirely, and native plus workflow commands get no deferral notice at all.

column8: A custom command that uses positional placeholders silently loses every argument. Concrete: `.nessy-agent/commands/migrate.md` containing `Migrate the $0 component from $1 to $2.`, invoked as `/migrate SearchBar React Vue` — the composer shows `/migrate SearchBar React Vue`, but the model-facing turn body is the unchanged sentence with literal `$0 $1 $2` (modelMessage replaces the visible message for the model, SessionManager.ts:15120-15121), so the model is asked to migrate a component named `$0` and never sees SearchBar/React/Vue at all. Same for an imported Claude plugin command written against `$1` (a common shape in the official catalogues): it installs with no visible warning — the `plugin.deferred.claude_command_dynamic_substitution` entry surfaces only inside the blocked-install toast (PluginsPage.tsx:1856), and a successful install never shows it — then behaves as if the user typed no arguments. `\$1.00` in prose also arrives with the backslash still attached. The same placeholders in a `/skill-name` invocation work correctly, which makes the failure look arbitrary to the user.

column5: The review ENGINE exists and is wired; the documented ENTRY POINT and four contract details do not. (1) No user-invocable command: `review` is model-invocable only, the exact inverse of the doc's `disable-model-invocation` (:339). (2) Wrong default scope: ours is uncommitted-only (review-tool.ts:83) where the doc's is "branch's commits ahead of its upstream plus any uncommitted changes" (:295) — an upstream-relative diff we never compute. (3) Narrower target grammar: `base` (merge-base) and `commit` only; no file path, no PR number, no `main...my-feature` ref range, and no `ultra`. (4) No `--fix` and no `--comment`; `--comment` has no underlying GitHub mechanism anywhere in the repo. (5) Foreground-only: `background: false` is hard-coded (review-tool.ts:316), so the doc's background-subagent default and its three named foreground fallbacks are all collapsed into the fallback. (6) Findings ride a different shape: our P0-P3 `title/body/priority/confidence` object rendered as text, not `ReportFindings`' `file/summary/failureScenario/category` (:312) — same information, incompatible keys, and no `category` slug. (7) Cleanup findings absent: the rubric flags introduced defects only, where :285 also binds "reuse, simplification, and efficiency cleanups". (8) No per-invocation effort argument (:324). Also a fork-internal contradiction: our docs-site documents `/review` as a built-in slash command and no such command exists.

column8: Concrete and doubly bad, because our own docs advertise the missing command. A user reads docs-site/content/core-concepts/interactions.md:41 ("**`/review`** runs a dedicated, adversarial code review of a diff"), types `/review` in the composer, and nothing command-like happens: `/review` is not in the `/` menu (slash-command-menu.tsx:17), it is not a session command (session-command.ts:38-57), so the literal string is sent to the model as prose. `/code-review` behaves the same. Whether a review actually runs is then up to the model deciding to call the `review` tool on its own. When it does, the user gets a review that is narrower than the page they may have read: it covers only uncommitted changes — a user who has committed their branch work and typed `/code-review` expecting the documented "commits ahead of upstream" scope gets "No changes to review" — it blocks the turn instead of running in the background, it never applies its own fixes, it cannot take a PR number or a `main...my-feature` range, it reports no reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups, and its findings arrive as a P0-P3 text block rather than a rendered findings list.

column5: Three deltas, all on the leading-run parse; none on argument expansion, which is already correct for a single skill.  1. RUN LENGTH. We match one command; the doc requires a run of up to six when the first is a skill. This is not a wrong key name or a wrong value — the loop does not exist, and the singular `customSlashCommandId` type makes it unrepresentable end to end.  2. ARGUMENT DISTRIBUTION. The doc gives the SAME trailing text to every expanded skill. Our nearest native equivalent, `[skill:...]` mentions, PARTITIONS text between markers instead: `runtimeSkillArguments` (`packages/shared/src/capabilities/runtime-skill-content.ts:606-617`) is "Arguments following the last matching `[skill:...]` reference, up to the next skill mention", so on `[skill:a] [skill:b] do XYZ` skill-a gets `""` and skill-b gets `do XYZ`. That partition semantics is CORRECT for the model-emitted path (`extractModelSkillInvocations`, `base-agent.ts:2166-2188`, where the model writes a distinct task per marker) and must not be changed. The stacked-command fix therefore has to emit the shared text after EACH marker — `[skill:a] do XYZ\n[skill:b] do XYZ` — which the existing partition logic then reads back as `do XYZ` for both. No edit to `runtime-skill-content.ts` is needed, and that is the load-bearing detail: the naive composition `[skill:a] [skill:b] do XYZ` would silently give the first skill empty arguments.  3. CAP AND STOP RULE. Neither exists, because there is no run to bound. The stop condition reduces cleanly to `custom:skill:`-prefixed membership of the composer's own command list (non-user-invocable skills never enter it, `custom-commands.ts:443`); the doc's forked-subagent clause has no analogue today and would only become live if a subagent skill mode is ever added.

column7: CROSSES THE RENDERER/SERVER WIRE BOUNDARY — a risk trigger in this repo. `RPC_CHANNELS.sessions.SEND_MESSAGE` is a positional-argument channel and its 7th parameter changes shape (`packages/server-core/src/handlers/rpc/sessions.ts:310`; client side `apps/electron/src/shared/types.ts:385`). Accepting `scalar | array` is what keeps an older client or the headless `nessy-server` path working; without that widening this is a breaking wire change. It is a WIRE change only, not a persistence change: no id array is written to a session file — the handler collapses everything into `message` and `modelMessage` before persistence, so no migration and no schema version bump. Also frozen: `packages/shared/src/agent/__tests__/adjacent-backend-frozen-contract.test.ts:653-681` plus its fixture `fixtures/adjacent-backends/rpc-and-backends.json:252` assert the exact positional call and a single resolved key; both must be extended, not replaced. column8: Observable today, in the Electron composer, on the exact input the doc names. A user who types `/write-tests /fix-issue 123` and presses Enter gets ONE skill loaded (`write-tests`) with the literal string `/fix-issue 123` as its arguments; the second skill's instructions never enter the turn. It fails silently and plausibly: the transcript shows `/write-tests /fix-issue 123`, the `/` menu lists both skills, and the model receives `/fix-issue` as prose, so it may or may not choose to emit `[skill:fix-issue]` itself on a later turn — meaning the user sometimes gets the second skill a turn late and sometimes not at all, with no error either way. Anyone following Claude's own skills documentation, or a plugin README that assumes stacking, hits this. Secondary surface: the argument text is also wrong for the one skill that does load — it receives `/fix-issue 123` instead of `123`, so a skill whose body uses `$1` or a declared argument name gets `/fix-issue` as its first positional value.

column5: Not a key-name-only mismatch — one of the three obligations is entirely absent and the other two are wrong in value and in unit. (1) DISK SPILL: absent. The doc requires the full output on disk and its path inside the truncated response; we write no file and the marker is a bare `[Output truncated to 32KB for the parent context.]` (subagent-tool.ts:177). The parent's only recourse is `get_subagent_result(agent_id)`, which is not the documented mechanism and by default returns 16 KiB — less than it already had. (2) TUNABILITY: absent. `OUTPUT_CAP_BYTES` is a hardcoded constant; `TASK_MAX_OUTPUT_LENGTH` (and any `NESSY_*` analogue) is unread, so the documented 160000 ceiling is unreachable. (3) UNIT: we count UTF-8 BYTES (32768) where the doc counts CHARACTERS (32000). ASCII output is near-parity (32768 vs 32000 chars, ours slightly larger); two-byte text — Cyrillic, which is this fork's primary locale — is cut at ~16 384 characters, roughly half the documented budget, and CJK/emoji worse. A separate consequence of the same fixed number: even if the cap became tunable, values above 64 KiB would do nothing, because the host's read-side `MAX_RESULT_BYTES = 64 * 1024` (child-session-service.ts:42) is what the inline path receives.
